questions.title: Resource Requests, Limits, and QoS Classes
questions.prompt: Explain what Kubernetes does differently with a Pod's `resources.requests` versus `resources.limits`, and how the combination of the two (or the absence of one) determines the Pod's QoS class (Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort). Why does that class matter when the node runs low on memory?
questions.modelAnswer: Requests are what the scheduler uses to place a Pod: it only schedules a Pod onto a node that has at least that much unreserved CPU/memory, and requests are what kubelet uses for CPU shares so the Pod gets a guaranteed minimum slice of CPU time. Limits are an enforced ceiling: for CPU, the kernel throttles the container via CFS quotas once it exceeds its limit; for memory, there is no throttling — exceeding the memory limit gets the container OOM-killed by the kernel cgroup controller, not by Kubernetes itself. If requests are left unset, Kubernetes treats the request as equal to zero, which lets the scheduler over-pack a node far beyond its real capacity. QoS class is derived mechanically from requests/limits: Guaranteed requires requests to equal limits (CPU and memory) on every container; Burstable means at least one request is set but requests != limits; BestEffort means no requests or limits are set at all. Under node memory pressure, the kubelet's eviction manager evicts BestEffort pods first, then Burstable pods (ranked by how far actual usage exceeds requested memory), and only evicts Guaranteed pods as an absolute last resort. This means QoS class is a direct, practical lever for workload priority during resource contention, not just a cosmetic label.
questions.professionalAnswer: Requests are basically 'what I need reserved to run,' and that's what the scheduler bin-packs the node against. Limits are the hard ceiling. On CPU that ceiling is soft in the sense that you just get throttled — your container slows down but keeps running. On memory there's no throttling at all; go over the limit and the kernel OOM-kills the container, full stop, and Kubernetes just reports that as an OOMKilled restart. The thing that trips people up is QoS class, because it's invisible unless you go looking for it — `kubectl describe pod` will show it. If requests equal limits everywhere, you're Guaranteed and you're the last thing evicted when a node is starved. If you only set requests, or requests don't match limits, you're Burstable. If you set neither, you're BestEffort, and when a node starts running out of memory, BestEffort pods get killed first, no questions asked. I've actually used that deliberately — batch jobs I don't mind losing get left BestEffort, and anything customer-facing gets requests==limits so it's protected.
questions.example: A Pod with requests.memory=256Mi, limits.memory=256Mi, requests.cpu=500m, limits.cpu=500m is Guaranteed. The same Pod with no `resources` block at all is BestEffort and is evicted first under node memory pressure.
commonMistakes: Assuming memory limits throttle like CPU limits, instead of causing an OOM-kill
Leaving requests unset and not realizing that defaults to zero for scheduling purposes, enabling node over-packing
Not connecting QoS class to actual eviction order under node pressure
Thinking QoS class is set explicitly in a field rather than derived from the requests/limits values
keyPoints: Requests drive scheduling placement and CPU share guarantees
CPU limit breaches throttle; memory limit breaches OOM-kill
QoS class (Guaranteed/Burstable/BestEffort) is derived from requests vs. limits
Eviction order under node pressure follows QoS class, BestEffort first

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes requests (scheduling) from limits (enforcement)
Correctly explains CPU throttling vs. memory OOM-kill behavior
Correctly derives QoS classes from requests/limits combinations
Connects QoS class to real eviction behavior under resource pressure

questions.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler vs. Cluster Autoscaler
questions.prompt: What is the division of responsibility between the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) and the Cluster Autoscaler in a Kubernetes cluster, and what has to be true for them to work well together rather than fight each other?
questions.modelAnswer: HPA operates at the Pod level: it watches a metric (by default CPU/memory utilization against requests, or custom/external metrics via the metrics API) for a target workload and changes the `replicas` count on a Deployment/StatefulSet to try to hold that metric near a target value. It never changes node count. Cluster Autoscaler operates at the node level: it watches for Pods that are unschedulable because no node has enough free capacity, and adds nodes (from a configured node pool/group) to fit them; it also watches for underutilized nodes whose Pods could be rescheduled elsewhere and removes those nodes to save cost. For the two to cooperate rather than conflict, every Pod HPA might create needs accurate resource requests set, because Cluster Autoscaler's scheduling simulation depends on requests, not actual usage, to decide whether a new Pod fits; if requests are missing or wrong, Cluster Autoscaler either over-provisions nodes or fails to add nodes a Pod genuinely needs. There also has to be budget in the node pool's max size for Cluster Autoscaler to actually scale out, and Pod Disruption Budgets matter because Cluster Autoscaler respects them when scaling down, so overly strict PDBs can prevent cost-saving scale-down even when nodes are genuinely idle.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of HPA as 'more copies of the same thing' and Cluster Autoscaler as 'more room to put things.' HPA looks at a metric — usually CPU against what you requested — and bumps replica count up or down. It has zero awareness of nodes; it'll happily ask for 20 replicas even if there's nowhere to put them. That's where Cluster Autoscaler comes in: it watches the scheduler's pending Pods, and if something's stuck unschedulable because nothing fits, it adds a node from whatever pool you've configured, as long as you haven't hit the pool's max size. The thing that breaks this pairing in practice is always the same: somebody forgets to set resource requests on the Deployment HPA is scaling. Cluster Autoscaler doesn't look at real usage, it does a scheduling simulation using requests — no requests means it can't tell if the new replica fits anywhere, so you get pods stuck Pending and nobody immediately understands why, because CPU usage on existing nodes looks fine. The other gotcha is PodDisruptionBudgets on scale-down — if your PDB says you can never go below N replicas available, Cluster Autoscaler won't evict the pods needed to drain and remove an idle node, so you end up paying for nodes that never get cleaned up.
questions.example: A Deployment with no CPU request set gets scaled to 20 replicas by HPA; Cluster Autoscaler can't determine if new nodes are needed because it has nothing to simulate against, and pods sit Pending.
commonMistakes: Believing HPA can add nodes, or Cluster Autoscaler can change replica counts
Omitting resource requests, which breaks Cluster Autoscaler's scheduling simulation
Ignoring node pool max-size limits that silently cap how far Cluster Autoscaler can scale out
Not accounting for PodDisruptionBudgets blocking scale-down of genuinely idle nodes
keyPoints: HPA scales replica count based on metrics; Cluster Autoscaler scales node count based on scheduling pressure
Cluster Autoscaler's decisions depend on accurate resource requests, not live usage
Node pool max size and PodDisruptionBudgets both gate whether Cluster Autoscaler can act
The two systems only cooperate correctly when requests are set honestly on every autoscaled workload

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates HPA's pod-level scope from Cluster Autoscaler's node-level scope
Explains that Cluster Autoscaler relies on requests, not actual usage
Identifies PDBs and node pool limits as real-world constraints on cooperation
Gives a concrete failure mode when the two are misconfigured together

questions.title: Why Remote State and Locking Exist in Terraform
questions.prompt: Explain why Terraform teams move away from local state files to a remote backend, and specifically what problem state locking solves that remote storage alone does not.
questions.modelAnswer: Local state (a `terraform.tfstate` file on one engineer's machine) creates two problems for a team: it isn't shared, so two engineers working from different checkouts have divergent views of what's deployed and will overwrite each other's state when they each run apply; and it isn't durable or protected, so a lost laptop or an accidental delete can destroy the only record Terraform has of what it's managing, forcing a painful re-import of every resource. A remote backend (e.g., an Azure Storage Account container, an S3 bucket) solves the sharing and durability problem by giving every engineer and every CI pipeline the same single source of truth, with versioning for recovery. Remote storage alone does not solve concurrency: if two `terraform apply` runs read the same remote state at the same time, both compute a plan against the same starting point, and whichever writes back last silently clobbers the other's changes, corrupting the state file's record of what exists. State locking adds a mutex layer on top of the remote backend (e.g., a lease on a blob, or a DynamoDB table used as a lock table for an S3 backend) so that a second `apply` attempting to run while a lock is held is blocked or fails fast, rather than racing. Locking is specifically about serializing concurrent writes; remote storage is about making the one true copy shared and durable.
questions.professionalAnswer: Local state is fine solo, but the second you're on a team it becomes a liability two different ways. First, it's just not shared — if I run apply from my laptop and you run apply from yours, we've each got our own stale copy of 'reality' and we're going to stomp on each other. Second, it's fragile — if that one file disappears, Terraform has literally lost its memory of everything it's managing, and recovering means importing every resource by hand, which is miserable. Remote backends fix both of those: everyone points at the same storage, and it's got versioning so you can roll back a bad state write. What people sometimes think remote state alone fixes, but doesn't, is the race condition — if you and I both happen to run `terraform apply` at the same moment, we're both reading the same state, computing our own plan against it, and whoever finishes and writes back last just overwrites the other person's result, state corruption, no error. Locking is the piece that actually prevents that — it's a mutex on top of the remote store, so the second apply either waits or gets told 'state is locked, try later' instead of racing silently.
questions.example: S3 backend + DynamoDB lock table: S3 holds the shared state file; DynamoDB provides the lock so a second concurrent `apply` fails with 'Error acquiring the state lock' instead of corrupting state.
commonMistakes: Conflating 'shared storage' with 'safe from concurrent writes' — they solve different problems
Not recognizing that a lost local state file effectively requires re-importing all managed resources
Assuming remote backends automatically include locking (some do, some require an explicit lock mechanism)
Underestimating how silent and damage-causing a lock-free concurrent apply race can be
keyPoints: Local state fails on both sharing (divergent views) and durability (single point of loss)
Remote backends provide a single shared, durable source of truth
Locking specifically prevents concurrent writes from racing and corrupting state
Locking and remote storage are complementary, not redundant

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the sharing and durability problems with local state
Correctly isolates locking as the solution to the concurrency/race problem specifically
Gives a concrete, correct example of a backend + lock mechanism
Communicates the distinction clearly without conflating the two concerns

questions.title: Module Input/Output Contracts and Versioning
questions.prompt: When you write a reusable Terraform module, what makes its variable and output definitions a real 'contract,' and why does module versioning matter once more than one team consumes that module?
questions.modelAnswer: A module's `variable` blocks define its required and optional inputs, including type constraints, defaults, and validation rules, and its `output` blocks define exactly what the module exposes back to callers. Together these form the module's public interface: a caller should never need to read the module's internal resource blocks to use it correctly, only its variables.tf and outputs.tf. This is a contract because changing it is a breaking change for every consumer — renaming a variable, tightening a type constraint, or removing an output breaks every root module calling it, the same way changing a function signature breaks every caller in software. Module versioning (pinning a Git tag, or a version constraint against a registry module) matters once more than one team or environment consumes a shared module because it lets consumers upgrade on their own schedule instead of being forced onto whatever the module author changes next: team A can stay on v1.2.0 of a networking module while team B adopts v2.0.0 with its new required variable, and the module author can evolve the module without silently breaking every existing caller at the next `terraform init`. Without pinned versions, a module sourced straight from a branch means every consumer gets every change the moment it merges, with no chance to review or test against it first.
questions.professionalAnswer: The variables and outputs are the only part of the module anyone calling it should ever have to look at — that's the whole point of a module. If I have to go read the internal resource blocks to know what I'm supposed to pass in, the module's interface has failed. And because it's a contract, changing it is exactly as risky as changing a function signature in a shared library — rename a variable, add a new required one with no default, or drop an output someone was referencing, and you've broken every root module that calls it, possibly without anyone noticing until an apply fails somewhere downstream. Versioning is what keeps that from being catastrophic once you've got more than one consumer. If I tag releases — v1.0.0, v1.1.0, v2.0.0 for the breaking change — then each team pins to whatever version they've tested against, and they upgrade when they're ready, not the instant I push a change. The anti-pattern I've seen bite teams is sourcing a module straight off a branch, like `git::...//modules/network?ref=main` — now every merge to main is effectively an instant, untested release to every consumer, and that's how one engineer's 'small refactor' takes down three other teams' environments in the same afternoon.
questions.example: Module v1.x exposes `output "subnet_id"`; v2.0.0 renames it to `output "subnet_ids"` (now a list) — a genuine breaking change that requires a major version bump so existing callers pinned to v1.x are unaffected until they choose to upgrade.
commonMistakes: Requiring consumers to read internal resource blocks to understand how to call the module
Changing variable names, types, or outputs without treating it as a breaking change
Sourcing shared modules from a mutable branch ref instead of a pinned tag/version
Not using semantic versioning to signal breaking vs. additive changes to consumers
keyPoints: Variables and outputs together form the module's public interface/contract
Changes to that interface are breaking changes for every consumer, just like a function signature
Version pinning lets independent teams upgrade on their own schedule
Sourcing from a mutable branch ref removes the safety versioning is meant to provide

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames variables/outputs as the module's interface contract
Explains why changing that interface is a breaking change for consumers
Correctly explains the role of versioning for independent, multi-team adoption
Identifies the risk of sourcing from a mutable branch ref

questions.title: DORA Metrics and What They Actually Measure
questions.prompt: Name the four DORA metrics and explain what each one is actually trying to capture about a software delivery process — and why a team can have excellent deployment frequency but still be performing poorly overall.
questions.modelAnswer: The four DORA metrics are: deployment frequency (how often code is successfully deployed to production), lead time for changes (the time from a commit being made to that commit running in production), change failure rate (the percentage of deployments that cause a failure in production requiring remediation, such as a rollback, hotfix, or incident), and time to restore service (how long it takes to recover from a production failure once it occurs). The first two measure throughput/speed, and the second two measure stability/quality; the DORA research's key finding is that high performers are good at both simultaneously, which contradicts the older assumption that speed and stability trade off against each other. A team can deploy extremely frequently (high deployment frequency, low lead time) while still performing poorly overall if a large fraction of those deployments break production (high change failure rate) and the team is slow to recover when they do (long time to restore service) — that combination describes a team moving fast but recklessly, shipping frequent incidents rather than frequent value, and DORA explicitly treats that as a failure mode, not a strength, because stability metrics are weighted just as heavily as speed metrics in classifying elite vs. low performers.
questions.professionalAnswer: The four are deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service. The first pair is basically 'how fast do we ship,' and the second pair is 'how often does shipping break things, and how fast do we fix it when it does.' The whole point of DORA's research, and why I actually care about it, is that it killed the old assumption that you have to trade speed for stability — the actual data says the best teams are fast and stable at the same time, it's not a seesaw. So if someone tells me 'we deploy 50 times a day,' that's not automatically good news. If change failure rate is high and time to restore is measured in hours, what they're really telling me is they ship incidents 50 times a day, and just happen to call that velocity. I've seen teams proudly report deployment frequency in a dashboard while quietly having no idea what their change failure rate is, because nobody's tracking rollbacks and hotfixes as a metric — and that's usually the tell that the 'fast' number is covering for a 'reckless' reality.
questions.example: Team reports 40 deploys/week (elite-tier frequency) but 35% of those require a hotfix or rollback within 24 hours (poor change failure rate) — DORA classifies this as a low performer overall, not elite, because stability is weighted equally.
commonMistakes: Naming only two or three of the four metrics, or conflating lead time with cycle time generically
Treating deployment frequency alone as sufficient evidence of good delivery performance
Assuming speed and stability are inherently a trade-off, contrary to DORA's actual finding
Not tracking change failure rate or time to restore at all, making the 'good news' metrics unverifiable
keyPoints: Four metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore service
First two measure throughput; last two measure stability/quality
Elite performers are strong on both dimensions simultaneously, not a trade-off
High frequency with high failure rate and slow recovery is a failure mode, not a strength

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names and defines all four DORA metrics
Correctly separates throughput metrics from stability metrics
Explains DORA's finding that speed and stability are not a trade-off for elite performers
Gives a coherent explanation of why high frequency alone can mask poor performance

questions.title: What GitHub Actions Caching Actually Saves (and Doesn't)
questions.prompt: Explain what `actions/cache` is doing under the hood in a GitHub Actions workflow, what a cache key and restore-keys fallback are for, and why a poorly chosen cache key can make builds slower or silently incorrect rather than faster.
questions.modelAnswer: `actions/cache` persists a directory (e.g., a package manager's dependency cache, or build output) to GitHub's cache storage keyed by a string you provide, and restores it on a later run if a cache entry with a matching key exists; this avoids re-downloading or re-building unchanged dependencies on every run. The cache key should be derived from something that changes exactly when the cached content needs to change — typically a hash of the lockfile (e.g., `hashFiles('**/package-lock.json')`) combined with the OS and a cache-format version, so a dependency change produces a new key and a dependency-identical run reuses the old one. `restore-keys` provides an ordered list of prefix fallbacks: if no exact key match exists, GitHub Actions restores the most recent cache matching a listed prefix, which is useful for restoring a 'close enough' cache (e.g., most dependencies unchanged) to speed up partial installs, but note that a restore-keys hit does not save a new cache entry under the exact key automatically — the job must still run and then save. A key chosen too broadly (e.g., keyed only on branch name, not on lockfile contents) will restore a stale cache after a dependency change, which can produce builds that silently use outdated dependencies rather than failing loudly; a key chosen too narrowly or non-deterministically (e.g., including a timestamp) never gets a cache hit at all and defeats the purpose, often making the job slower than no caching because of the overhead of attempting to restore and re-save a cache every run.
questions.professionalAnswer: What it's really doing is just: save this folder to GitHub's storage under a key, and next time, if a cache with that exact key exists, pull it down instead of rebuilding from scratch. The key is everything here — it should change exactly when the thing you're caching should change, which in practice usually means hashing the lockfile. If the lockfile hash is the same, your dependencies haven't changed, reuse the cache; if it changed, you need a new cache. `restore-keys` is the fallback list — if there's no exact match, grab the newest cache matching one of these prefixes, which is handy for 'most things didn't change, give me a head start' even if it's not a perfect hit. The mistake I've actually seen cost people real time debugging: someone keys the cache off the branch name instead of the lockfile hash. Looks fine for weeks, then someone bumps a dependency version on that branch, the cache key doesn't change because it's still the same branch name, and the build silently restores the old dependency set — no error, just quietly wrong, until something breaks in a way that doesn't make sense until you realize the cache never invalidated. The other version of getting it wrong is going too aggressive the other way — sticking a timestamp or run ID in the key — now you never get a hit, ever, and you've added the overhead of a cache restore attempt and a cache save step to every single run for literally zero benefit.
questions.example: Good key: `${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}` — changes exactly when dependencies change. Bad key: `${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ github.ref }}` — stays the same across dependency bumps on the same branch, silently serving a stale cache.
commonMistakes: Keying the cache on something that doesn't change when the cached content should (e.g., branch name instead of lockfile hash)
Including a non-deterministic value (timestamp, run ID) in the key, guaranteeing a permanent cache miss
Assuming a restore-keys fallback hit is equivalent to an exact match rather than a 'close enough' partial restore
Not understanding that a stale cache can silently serve outdated dependencies rather than erroring
keyPoints: Cache key should derive from content that changes exactly when invalidation is needed (e.g., lockfile hash)
restore-keys provides ordered prefix fallbacks for partial/approximate cache hits
An overly broad key causes silent staleness; an overly narrow/non-deterministic key causes permanent misses
Caching is a performance optimization that can introduce correctness risk if keyed incorrectly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the mechanics of cache key matching and storage
Correctly explains restore-keys as ordered prefix fallbacks
Identifies the silent-staleness risk from an overly broad key
Identifies the permanent-miss risk from an overly narrow/non-deterministic key

questions.title: Prometheus's Pull Model and Why rate() Needs a Counter
questions.prompt: Explain why Prometheus scrapes metrics (a pull model) rather than having applications push metrics to it, and explain what the `rate()` function does with a counter metric and why using `rate()` on a gauge produces nonsense.
questions.modelAnswer: Prometheus's server actively scrapes an HTTP `/metrics` endpoint on each target at a configured interval, rather than targets pushing to Prometheus. This pull model gives Prometheus direct control over scrape timing and the ability to detect a target as down simply by a failed scrape (an implicit health signal, `up == 0`), and it avoids targets needing to know Prometheus's network address or implement retry/backoff logic for delivery — the server does the work of reaching out. It also makes local testing trivial, since a target's `/metrics` endpoint can be curled directly. Counters are metrics that only increase (or reset to zero on restart), such as total HTTP requests served. `rate()` computes the per-second average rate of increase of a counter over a time window by looking at the difference between samples and dividing by the time elapsed, automatically handling counter resets (if the value is lower than the previous sample, it assumes a reset and adjusts rather than reporting a negative rate). Gauges are metrics that can go up or down, such as current memory usage or current queue depth; applying `rate()` to a gauge is semantically meaningless because `rate()`'s reset-detection logic assumes monotonic increase, so a legitimate decrease in a gauge's value gets misinterpreted as a counter reset, producing an inflated and incorrect rate. The correct function family for gauges is `deriv()` or simply direct value comparison, not `rate()`.
questions.professionalAnswer: Pull makes sense once you think about it operationally: Prometheus reaches out to each target's `/metrics` endpoint on its own schedule, so it's in control of when and how often, and — this is the underrated part — a failed scrape is itself a signal. If Prometheus can't reach a target, that's `up == 0`, free health-check data, no extra instrumentation needed. With a push model you'd need the app to know where to send data, handle retries if the collector's down, and you lose that clean 'can't reach it' signal because the app just silently fails to push and you might not notice for a while. On `rate()` — counters only go up, so `rate()` is just 'how fast is this increasing per second,' and it's smart enough to notice if the raw value dropped between samples and treat that as a restart/reset rather than reporting a negative rate, which would be nonsense. The actual gotcha is people running `rate()` on a gauge, like current memory usage — a gauge going down is completely normal, memory gets freed all the time, but `rate()`'s reset-detection logic sees that drop and 'corrects' for it as if it were a counter reset, and you get this garbage inflated number that doesn't mean anything. I've watched people build an entire alert off a `rate()` on a gauge and wonder why it fires randomly — the function is just the wrong tool for that metric type.
questions.example: `rate(http_requests_total[5m])` on a counter correctly yields requests/second. `rate(node_memory_available_bytes[5m])` on a gauge produces a misleading value because normal decreases are misread as counter resets.
commonMistakes: Assuming push would be strictly simpler without recognizing the lost 'target unreachable' health signal
Applying rate() to a gauge metric
Not understanding that rate() automatically compensates for counter resets (e.g., process restarts)
Confusing counters (monotonic) with gauges (can increase or decrease) when choosing instrumentation types
keyPoints: Prometheus pulls metrics via scheduled scrapes, giving it control and an implicit health signal
Counters are monotonically increasing; rate() computes per-second increase and compensates for resets
Gauges can rise or fall; applying rate() to them produces meaningless, often inflated results
Correct function choice depends on correctly identifying the metric type

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the pull model and its operational benefits
Correctly explains rate()'s behavior on counters, including reset handling
Correctly explains why rate() on a gauge is semantically wrong
Communicates the distinction clearly with a concrete example

questions.title: SLIs, SLOs, and Error Budgets
questions.prompt: Define SLI, SLO, and error budget, and explain the practical decision an error budget is meant to drive — what should a team actually do differently once they've burned through most of their error budget for the period?
questions.modelAnswer: An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a quantitative measurement of some aspect of service behavior, such as the proportion of HTTP requests served successfully within 300ms. An SLO (Service Level Objective) is a target value or range for that SLI over a period, such as '99.9% of requests succeed within 300ms, measured over a rolling 30 days.' The error budget is the complement of the SLO expressed as an allowance: if the SLO is 99.9%, the error budget is the remaining 0.1% of requests/time that are allowed to fail or be slow before the SLO is breached, and it is typically tracked as a consumable quantity over the period rather than just a pass/fail state. The practical decision an error budget is meant to drive is a release-and-risk-taking policy: when a team has budget remaining, they can ship features, take calculated risks, and even tolerate planned risky changes, because they have room to absorb some failure; once the budget is mostly or fully consumed, the team is expected to shift priority toward reliability work — freezing risky releases, prioritizing bug fixes and resilience work, and deferring new feature launches — until the budget replenishes in the next period. This converts an abstract reliability target into an objective, pre-agreed trigger for a concrete behavior change, removing the need for an argument every time reliability and feature velocity are in tension.
questions.professionalAnswer: SLI is just a number you're measuring — like, 'what percentage of requests came back under 300ms successfully.' SLO is the target for that number — '99.9% over a rolling 30 days.' Error budget is the flip side of that target expressed as an allowance — if your SLO is 99.9%, your budget is the 0.1% you're allowed to blow through before you're out of compliance, and the useful part is treating that like a number that drains over the period, not just a binary 'are we green or red.' The actual point of having one — and this is the part people miss if they just report the SLO number without using it — is that it's supposed to be a pre-agreed trigger for behavior. When you've got budget left, ship fast, take the risky migration, push the experimental feature flag to 100%, whatever — you've got room to absorb a mistake. Once you've burned through most of it, the agreed behavior flips: no more risky releases, feature work gets deprioritized, and the team's actual job for the rest of the period is closing reliability gaps, not shipping the next thing. The value of having agreed to this ahead of time is that nobody has to have an argument in the moment about whether 'just one more release' is okay — the budget already answered that question before anyone was emotionally invested in shipping their feature today.
questions.example: SLO: 99.9% of requests succeed within 300ms over 30 days. If actual performance has been running at 99.92% with 25 days left in the period, the team has effectively used most of its budget and should pause risky deploys rather than ship another experimental feature.
commonMistakes: Defining SLI, SLO, and error budget correctly in the abstract but not connecting error budget to an actual behavior change
Treating the SLO as a simple pass/fail rather than tracking budget consumption continuously over the period
Not recognizing that the point of a pre-agreed budget policy is to remove in-the-moment negotiation over releases
Confusing SLI (the measurement) with SLO (the target) when asked to define them
keyPoints: SLI is the measured indicator; SLO is the target for that indicator over a period
Error budget is the allowed amount of non-compliance, tracked as a consumable quantity
Remaining budget licenses risk-taking; exhausted budget triggers a shift to reliability-focused work
The budget's value is as a pre-agreed, objective trigger, removing ad hoc negotiation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines SLI, SLO, and error budget
Correctly explains error budget as a consumable quantity over a period
Explains the concrete behavior change triggered by budget exhaustion
Articulates why a pre-agreed policy is more valuable than ad hoc judgment calls

questions.title: Least Privilege and Workload Identity
questions.prompt: Explain the principle of least privilege as applied to a CI/CD pipeline or a running workload, and explain what 'workload identity' is and why it's considered a stronger practice than embedding a long-lived cloud credential or service account key in the pipeline or container.
questions.modelAnswer: Least privilege means granting an identity (a person, a pipeline, or a running workload) only the specific permissions it needs to perform its function, and nothing more — a deployment pipeline that only ever creates resources in one resource group should not hold subscription-wide Owner rights, even if that would be more convenient. The practical benefit is blast-radius reduction: if that identity's credential is ever leaked or the pipeline is compromised, the attacker is limited to whatever that narrow permission set allows, not the whole environment. Workload identity (e.g., Azure Workload Identity Federation, AWS IAM roles for service accounts/IRSA) is a mechanism that lets a workload (a Kubernetes Pod, a GitHub Actions job) exchange a short-lived, automatically-rotated token — typically backed by OIDC federation between the workload's own identity provider and the cloud provider's IAM — for temporary cloud credentials, instead of having a long-lived secret (a service account key file, a static access key) baked into the container image, a Kubernetes Secret, or pipeline configuration. This is considered stronger because long-lived credentials are a standing liability: they don't expire on their own, they can be copied and exfiltrated and keep working indefinitely until someone notices and manually revokes them, and they're easy to accidentally leak into logs, images, or version control. Federated workload identity tokens are short-lived, scoped to the specific workload's identity, and require no secret to ever be stored at rest at all, which removes an entire class of leak vectors.
questions.professionalAnswer: Least privilege is the boring-sounding but actually load-bearing idea that a pipeline or a workload should only be able to do the one thing it's supposed to do. If my deploy pipeline only ever touches one resource group, it should have a role scoped to that resource group, not subscription Owner, even though Owner would mean I never have to think about permissions again. The reason that discipline matters is blast radius — if that pipeline's credential leaks, which happens more than anyone likes to admit, the damage is capped at whatever that narrow role can do, not 'attacker now owns the whole subscription.' Workload identity is the mechanism that makes 'no long-lived credential at all' actually practical. Instead of baking a service account key or an access key into a container or a pipeline secret, the workload — a Pod, a GitHub Actions job — proves who it is via its own identity provider, usually OIDC, and trades that for a short-lived cloud token on the fly. No secret ever sits at rest anywhere waiting to be leaked. I've seen the alternative go wrong plenty of times — someone commits a service account JSON key to a repo by accident, or it sits in a Kubernetes Secret that gets dumped in a support ticket, and that key just keeps working until someone remembers to rotate it, which could be months. A federated token is gone in an hour even if someone manages to grab it mid-flight.
questions.example: A GitHub Actions workflow using OIDC federation to assume an AWS IAM role gets a credential valid for roughly an hour, scoped to exactly the actions the role allows — versus a static AWS access key stored as a repo secret that remains valid indefinitely until someone manually rotates it.
commonMistakes: Granting broad roles (Owner/Contributor at a high scope) for convenience instead of scoping to the minimum needed
Storing long-lived keys in pipeline secrets or container images instead of using federated identity
Not recognizing that a leaked long-lived credential remains valid until manually revoked
Treating workload identity as merely 'more convenient' rather than a genuine reduction in standing risk
keyPoints: Least privilege scopes an identity's permissions to exactly what it needs, limiting blast radius
Workload identity federates a workload's own identity to obtain short-lived cloud credentials on demand
Long-lived credentials are a standing liability — they don't expire and can be exfiltrated silently
Federated identity removes the need to store any secret at rest

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains least privilege with a concrete pipeline/workload example
Correctly explains the workload identity federation mechanism
Clearly articulates why long-lived credentials are riskier than federated short-lived tokens
Communicates with a concrete, realistic failure scenario

questions.title: What an SBOM Is and Why Supply Chain Risk Needs One
questions.prompt: Explain what a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) actually contains, and walk through why having one matters when a new CVE is disclosed in a widely used open-source library.
questions.modelAnswer: An SBOM is a structured, machine-readable inventory of every component that makes up a piece of software — direct dependencies, their transitive dependencies, versions, licenses, and often cryptographic hashes — typically produced in a standard format such as SPDX or CycloneDX, generated at build time from the actual dependency graph rather than from documentation. It is the software equivalent of an ingredients list: it tells you precisely what is inside a given build artifact, not what the developers believe is inside it. When a new CVE is disclosed in a widely used library, the practical problem an organization faces is not 'is this library vulnerable' but 'which of the hundreds of applications we run actually include that library, at that vulnerable version, and is it a direct or deeply transitive dependency.' Without SBOMs, answering that requires manually auditing source trees or lockfiles across every repository and every deployed artifact, which is slow and error-prone, especially for transitive dependencies nobody on the team explicitly chose. With SBOMs generated for every build and stored queryable, the organization can run a single query across its SBOM inventory for the affected package name and vulnerable version range, get back an authoritative list of every affected artifact in minutes, and prioritize remediation by actual exposure rather than guesswork. This turns incident response for a supply-chain CVE from a multi-day audit into a lookup.
questions.professionalAnswer: An SBOM is literally the ingredients list for your software — every direct dependency, every dependency of a dependency, versions, licenses, usually hashes, generated straight off the real build, not off what someone wrote in a README. The value only becomes obvious the day a CVE drops in something like a widely used logging library. The question everyone's suddenly asking is 'are we affected,' and that's actually two much harder questions: which of our however-many services even pull this library in, and at what version, including the ones that pulled it in as some third library's dependency that nobody on the team ever consciously chose. If you don't have SBOMs, that's a scramble — people grepping lockfiles, pinging teams, hoping someone remembers. If you do have SBOMs generated for every build and sitting somewhere queryable, it's one query: 'show me every artifact containing package X between versions Y and Z,' and you've got your exposure list in minutes instead of days. I think of SBOMs as insurance you pay for before you need it — nobody feels the benefit the week you set it up, but the first real supply-chain incident, it's the difference between an afternoon of targeted patching and a week of frantic, incomplete auditing.
questions.example: Log4Shell-style disclosure: with SBOMs on file for every build, a query for `log4j-core` in the vulnerable version range returns every affected artifact across the org in minutes; without SBOMs, teams must manually search dependency trees repo by repo.
commonMistakes: Describing an SBOM as documentation written by developers rather than a build-time-generated artifact
Not connecting SBOMs to transitive (indirect) dependencies, which are the hardest to track manually
Treating SBOM generation as a compliance checkbox rather than an operational tool used during incident response
Failing to mention the need for SBOMs to be queryable/searchable across the whole artifact inventory, not just stored
keyPoints: SBOM is a build-time-generated, machine-readable inventory of all direct and transitive components
It captures what's actually in the artifact, not what's documented or assumed
The real value surfaces during a supply-chain CVE: turning exposure discovery from a manual audit into a query
SBOMs need to be generated for every build and kept queryable to be useful during an incident

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines what an SBOM contains and how it's generated
Correctly explains the transitive dependency visibility problem it solves
Walks through the concrete CVE-response scenario clearly
Notes the operational requirement that SBOMs be queryable, not just archived

questions.title: Writing a Zero-Downtime Rolling Update Strategy
questions.prompt: You own a Deployment for a customer-facing API currently running 6 replicas. Write the `strategy` section (and any related fields) of the Deployment manifest so that a rollout never drops available capacity below 5 running, healthy replicas and never runs more than 8 pods at once during the rollout. Briefly explain your maxUnavailable/maxSurge choice.
questions.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
spec:
  replicas: 6
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
      maxSurge: 2
  # ...
questions.modelAnswer: With 6 replicas, `maxUnavailable: 1` and `maxSurge: 2` satisfies both constraints. maxUnavailable is expressed as a count or percentage of desired replicas that may be unavailable during the rollout; with 6 replicas, maxUnavailable: 1 guarantees at least 5 are available at any point (6 - 1 = 5), meeting the 'never below 5' requirement. maxSurge controls how many extra pods beyond the desired count may be created to speed up the rollout; maxSurge: 2 means the total running pod count during rollout can reach 6 + 2 = 8, meeting the 'never more than 8' requirement exactly. The rollout proceeds by creating new-version pods up to the surge ceiling, waiting for them to pass readiness probes, then terminating old-version pods up to the unavailable ceiling, cycling until complete — so the readiness probe configuration on the pod template is just as load-bearing as these two numbers, since Kubernetes only counts a pod as 'available' once it passes readiness, not just once it starts.
questions.professionalAnswer: For 6 replicas, I'd set maxUnavailable: 1 and maxSurge: 2. The way I check my own math here: maxUnavailable eats into your floor, so 6 minus 1 is 5 — that's my 'never below 5' guaranteed. maxSurge adds to your ceiling, so 6 plus 2 is 8 — that's my 'never above 8.' Both constraints land exactly on the numbers I was given, which tells me this is probably what the person asking intended. One thing I'd flag out loud in review: these numbers are only as good as the readiness probe backing them, because Kubernetes doesn't count a new pod as 'up' for rollout-accounting purposes until it passes readiness — if the readiness probe is too lenient (reports ready before the app can actually serve traffic), this whole careful maxUnavailable/maxSurge math doesn't protect you from a real capacity dip, it just protects you from a Kubernetes-reported one.
questions.example: During rollout: at most 8 total pods running (6 desired + 2 surge), at least 5 counted available at any moment (6 desired - 1 unavailable) — exactly matching the stated constraints.
commonMistakes: Setting maxUnavailable too high, dropping below the required floor of available replicas
Setting maxSurge too high, exceeding the stated pod count ceiling
Forgetting that 'available' depends on the pod's readiness probe passing, not just the container starting
Expressing maxUnavailable/maxSurge as percentages without checking they round to the exact counts required
keyPoints: maxUnavailable determines the floor of available replicas during rollout
maxSurge determines the ceiling of total running pods during rollout
Both values must be checked against the specific replica count given, not assumed as defaults
Readiness probes gate what counts as 'available' for rollout accounting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct maxUnavailable value satisfying the floor requirement
Correct maxSurge value satisfying the ceiling requirement
Correctly explains the arithmetic connecting the values to the constraints
Notes the dependency on readiness probes for accurate availability accounting

questions.title: Setting Requests/Limits and an HPA for a Bursty Workload
questions.prompt: A web API's CPU usage is normally around 150m per pod but spikes to 800m under load. Write the `resources` block for the container and an HPA manifest that keeps average CPU utilization near 60% of requested CPU, scaling between 3 and 15 replicas.
questions.code:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 1000m
    memory: 512Mi
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web-api-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web-api
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 15
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 60
questions.modelAnswer: Requests should be set a bit above the normal steady-state usage (150m) rather than exactly at it, since HPA utilization percentage is calculated against requests, and setting requests too close to typical usage causes the HPA to scale on normal noise; 250m gives headroom so 60% utilization corresponds to roughly 150m actual usage, matching the described steady state and leaving room to detect real spikes. The limit (1000m) should comfortably cover the peak (800m) with some margin to avoid throttling during the spike itself, since CPU throttling under load would make the spike worse, not better. minReplicas: 3 keeps a baseline for availability and load distribution even during the quietest periods; maxReplicas: 15 caps cost/blast radius during a runaway spike or feedback loop, and should be sized against real cluster/node pool capacity so the Cluster Autoscaler (if present) can actually provide nodes for 15 replicas' worth of requests. The HPA's `averageUtilization: 60` target means HPA tries to keep the average CPU usage across all replicas at 60% of requested CPU (60% of 250m = 150m), which aligns the trigger threshold with the described normal-vs-spike behavior.
questions.professionalAnswer: I set requests at 250m, a bit above the normal 150m, deliberately — if I set requests at exactly 150m, then normal operation is already sitting near 100% utilization relative to requests, and HPA would be twitchy, scaling up and down on ordinary noise instead of real spikes. With requests at 250m, normal 150m usage reads as 60% utilization, which conveniently is also my target — so HPA sits calm at baseline and only reacts when things actually change. Limits I put at 1000m, comfortably above the known 800m peak, because I don't want the pod getting throttled exactly when it's under the most load — that would just make a bad moment worse. For replica bounds, 3 minimum keeps some baseline spread for availability even at 3am with zero traffic, and 15 maximum caps how far this can run away — though I'd double check with whoever owns the node pool that 15 replicas' worth of CPU requests can actually be scheduled, because an HPA max that the cluster can't physically satisfy just means pods sit Pending instead of actually helping under load.
questions.example: At steady state (150m actual usage against 250m requested), HPA sees ~60% utilization and holds replica count steady; under a spike toward 800m per pod, utilization climbs well above 60% and HPA scales out toward the 15-replica ceiling.
commonMistakes: Setting requests too close to normal usage, making HPA react to routine noise
Setting limits too close to the known peak, risking throttling during the exact moment of highest load
Picking replica bounds without checking actual cluster/node pool capacity to support the maximum
Choosing a utilization target that doesn't correspond sensibly to the described normal-vs-peak behavior
keyPoints: Requests should sit above typical steady-state usage to avoid HPA reacting to normal noise
Limits should cover the known peak with margin to avoid throttling during load spikes
Replica min/max should reflect both business availability needs and real cluster capacity
The averageUtilization target should be checked against requests to confirm it aligns with described behavior

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Resource requests/limits are reasonable given the stated normal/peak usage
HPA manifest correctly targets CPU utilization at 60% with min 3 / max 15
Explains the relationship between requests and HPA utilization percentage
Notes the need to validate replica ceiling against real cluster capacity

questions.title: Writing a Reusable Terraform Module Call with Variables
questions.prompt: Write a `variables.tf` for a reusable Terraform module named `azure-resource-group` that accepts a required `name`, a required `location`, and an optional `tags` map defaulting to an empty map — then write the module call from a root module that uses it to create a resource group named `rg-payments-prod` in `eastus2` with a `tags` map containing `environment = "prod"`.
questions.modelAnswer: The variables.tf declares each input with an explicit `type` constraint, which causes Terraform to fail fast at plan time with a clear error if a caller passes the wrong shape (e.g., a string where a map is expected) rather than failing deep inside the module's resource logic. `name` and `location` are left without a `default`, which makes them required — Terraform will refuse to plan without them being supplied by the caller. `tags` has `default = {}`, making it optional; callers who don't care about tags can omit it entirely and the module still works. The root module call passes `name` and `location` as required positional-style arguments and supplies `tags` explicitly since the scenario calls for a specific tag. The module's own `main.tf` (not shown) would reference `var.name`, `var.location`, and `var.tags` when constructing the `azurerm_resource_group` resource, and would typically also expose an `output "id"` so callers can reference the created resource group's ID elsewhere.
questions.professionalAnswer: I keep this simple and deliberate: `name` and `location` get no default, because a resource group with no name or region doesn't mean anything — I want Terraform to refuse to run rather than silently inventing one. `tags` gets `default = {}` because tagging is a nice-to-have most callers should be able to skip without the module complaining at them. Typing everything explicitly (`string`, `map(string)`) isn't just tidiness — it means if someone passes `tags = "prod"` by mistake instead of a map, they get a clear type error at plan time, not some confusing failure three resources deep once Terraform tries to iterate over a string like it's a map. For the root call, I just pass what the scenario actually asked for — `rg-payments-prod`, `eastus2`, and the one tag — and I'd expect the module's own output block to hand back the resource group ID so anything else in the root module, like a virtual network resource, can reference `module.payments_rg.id` instead of hardcoding the name again somewhere else.
questions.example: A caller invoking the module without supplying `tags` still succeeds because of the default `{}`; a caller omitting `name` fails at `terraform plan` with a clear 'required variable not set' error.
commonMistakes: Giving name/location a default value, which would hide a caller's mistake of omitting a real name or region
Omitting type constraints, allowing a caller to pass the wrong data shape without an early error
Not setting tags to default to an empty map, forcing every caller to supply tags even when unnecessary
Hardcoding values inside the module instead of parameterizing them as variables
keyPoints: Required inputs (name, location) have no default, forcing callers to supply them
Optional input (tags) has a sensible empty-map default
Explicit type constraints catch caller mistakes early, at plan time
The root module call supplies exactly the values described in the scenario

evaluationCriteria.criterion: variables.tf correctly defines name/location as required, typed string variables
variables.tf correctly defines tags as an optional map(string) defaulting to {}
Root module call correctly supplies name, location, and the specified tag
Explanation correctly describes why type constraints and defaults matter

questions.title: Configuring a Remote Backend With State Locking on Azure
questions.prompt: Write the Terraform `backend` configuration block to store state in an Azure Storage Account container, including the elements needed so that concurrent `apply` runs are safely serialized.
questions.modelAnswer: The `azurerm` backend block points Terraform at a specific blob (`key`) inside a specific container (`container_name`) within a specific storage account (`storage_account_name`), which together identify the single shared state file this configuration manages. Unlike some backends that require a separate lock table, the azurerm backend provides state locking natively using blob lease functionality on the storage account — when `terraform apply` or `plan` runs, it acquires a lease on the state blob, and a second concurrent run attempting to acquire the same lease is blocked (or fails with a clear 'state is locked' error) until the first releases it, which is exactly the serialization needed to prevent concurrent writes from corrupting state. The `key` should be scoped per environment/workload (here, `payments/prod.terraform.tfstate`) so that different environments or components don't share a single state file and risk one team's apply affecting an unrelated state. Backend configuration values containing secrets (like an access key, if not using Azure AD auth) should not be hardcoded in version control; they're typically supplied via environment variables or a partial backend config completed at `terraform init` time.
questions.professionalAnswer: This points Terraform at one specific blob inside one specific container inside one specific storage account — that blob is the shared state file everyone and every pipeline reads and writes. What's nice about the azurerm backend specifically is you don't need a separate lock table like you would with some other backends — it just uses a blob lease on that same state blob for locking, so when someone runs apply, Terraform grabs a lease, and if a second apply tries to run at the same time, it just gets told the state's locked and has to wait or fail, instead of both racing to write. The `key` is the part I'd be most careful about in a real setup — I scope it per environment and per component, like `payments/prod.terraform.tfstate`, specifically so that prod and staging, or payments and some unrelated service, never accidentally share one state file. I'd also flag that none of this block should contain an actual access key in plain text committed to the repo — authentication to the storage account itself should go through Azure AD / managed identity or environment variables supplied at init time, not a secret sitting in version control next to the backend config.
questions.example: Two engineers running `terraform apply` on the same config at the same time: the second one's `apply` fails immediately with 'Error acquiring the state lock,' rather than silently racing against the first and corrupting the state file.
commonMistakes: Not scoping the state key per environment/component, risking shared state across unrelated workloads
Assuming the azurerm backend needs a separate external lock table like some other backends do
Hardcoding an access key or secret directly in the backend block in version control
Not recognizing that the lease mechanism is what actually prevents concurrent-apply corruption
keyPoints: Backend block fully identifies the single shared state blob (storage account, container, key)
The azurerm backend provides native locking via blob lease, no separate lock table needed
State key should be scoped per environment/component to avoid cross-contamination
Secrets for backend authentication should not be hardcoded in version control

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, complete azurerm backend block with resource group, storage account, container, key
Correctly explains the blob-lease locking mechanism and its concurrency-safety role
Notes the importance of scoping the state key per environment/component
Flags not hardcoding secrets in the backend configuration

questions.title: Writing a GitHub Actions Matrix Build With Dependency Caching
questions.prompt: Write a GitHub Actions workflow job that runs a Python test suite across Python versions 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12, and caches pip dependencies keyed so that a dependency change correctly invalidates the cache per Python version.
questions.code:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
      - uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/pip
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-py${{ matrix.python-version }}-pip-${{ hashFiles('requirements.txt') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-py${{ matrix.python-version }}-pip-
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest
questions.modelAnswer: The `strategy.matrix.python-version` array causes GitHub Actions to run the job three times in parallel, once per listed version, with `matrix.python-version` substitutable into each step. The cache key includes `runner.os`, the specific `matrix.python-version`, and a hash of `requirements.txt`, which is essential: including the Python version in the key prevents a 3.10-built cache from being incorrectly restored and reused for a 3.12 run (since compiled wheels and resolved dependency sets can differ by interpreter version), and including the requirements hash ensures a dependency change produces a new key, forcing a fresh install rather than reusing stale cached packages. `restore-keys` is scoped per Python version too (not shared across versions), so a cache miss on the exact requirements hash still prefers a same-version partial match over no match at all, rather than falling back to an unrelated Python version's cache. Without the per-version component in the key, all three matrix jobs would share one cache slot and overwrite each other, likely causing incorrect or inconsistent dependency resolution for at least two of the three versions.
questions.professionalAnswer: Matrix just runs this job three times in parallel, once per Python version listed, and `matrix.python-version` is how I reference 'whichever one this run is' inside the steps. The caching key is where I'd actually slow down and think, because the easy mistake here is keying the cache only on the requirements hash and forgetting the Python version entirely — if I did that, all three matrix jobs would be fighting over the exact same cache slot, and whichever one finishes first would effectively poison the cache for the other two, since compiled packages and resolved versions aren't guaranteed to be interchangeable across 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12. So the version goes in the key right alongside the requirements hash. The restore-keys fallback I also scope to the same Python version — no point falling back to a 3.10 partial cache on a 3.12 run, that's not 'close enough,' it's just wrong. Doing this correctly means a requirements.txt change invalidates the cache for all three versions independently and correctly, and the three matrix jobs never step on each other's cached dependencies.
questions.example: Changing a single pinned version in requirements.txt produces a new hash, which changes the cache key for all three matrix legs simultaneously, forcing a correct fresh install on each rather than three jobs silently sharing or fighting over one stale cache entry.
commonMistakes: Omitting matrix.python-version from the cache key, causing the three matrix jobs to collide on one cache slot
Omitting the requirements hash from the key, serving a stale dependency cache after a real dependency change
Using a restore-keys fallback that isn't scoped per Python version, risking cross-version 'close enough' restores that are actually wrong
Not understanding that matrix jobs run as fully independent job instances, each needing its own correctly scoped cache
keyPoints: Matrix strategy runs the job once per listed Python version, in parallel
Cache key must include both the Python version and the requirements hash to avoid cross-version collisions and staleness
restore-keys fallback should remain scoped to the same Python version
Each matrix leg needs its own correctly isolated cache, not a shared one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct matrix strategy covering all three specified Python versions
Cache key correctly includes both Python version and requirements hash
restore-keys correctly scoped per Python version rather than globally
Explanation correctly identifies the cross-version cache collision risk

questions.title: Writing an Azure DevOps Multi-Stage Release Pipeline With Approvals
questions.prompt: Write an Azure DevOps YAML pipeline with three stages — Dev, Staging, and Production — where Dev deploys automatically after a successful build, Staging requires the Dev stage to succeed first, and Production requires a manual approval gate before deployment.
questions.code:
stages:
  - stage: Build
    jobs:
      - job: BuildJob
        steps:
          - script: echo "build and publish artifact"

  - stage: Dev
    dependsOn: Build
    jobs:
      - deployment: DeployDev
        environment: dev
        strategy:
          runOnce:
            deploy:
              steps:
                - script: echo "deploy to dev"

  - stage: Staging
    dependsOn: Dev
    jobs:
      - deployment: DeployStaging
        environment: staging
        strategy:
          runOnce:
            deploy:
              steps:
                - script: echo "deploy to staging"

  - stage: Production
    dependsOn: Staging
    jobs:
      - deployment: DeployProduction
        environment: production   # 'production' environment has a manual-approval check configured
        strategy:
          runOnce:
            deploy:
              steps:
                - script: echo "deploy to production"
questions.modelAnswer: The pipeline uses `dependsOn` to chain stages in order (Dev depends on Build, Staging depends on Dev, Production depends on Staging), which enforces the required sequencing and means a failure anywhere upstream stops the pipeline from proceeding to later stages. Each deployment stage targets a named `environment` (dev, staging, production); Azure DevOps environments carry their own configurable approval and check policies independent of the YAML file itself — the manual approval gate for Production is not written as YAML logic but configured on the `production` environment resource in the Azure DevOps project settings (Approvals and Checks), which means the pipeline author needs write access to the environment, not just the pipeline, to actually enforce it. Dev has no approval configured on its environment, so it proceeds automatically the moment the Build stage succeeds; Staging likewise proceeds automatically once Dev succeeds, assuming no approval is configured there either. This separation (sequencing in YAML, gating policy on the environment object) is intentional: it lets the approval policy be changed by whoever owns environment security without needing a pipeline code change or a PR.
questions.professionalAnswer: The sequencing is all `dependsOn` — Dev depends on Build, Staging depends on Dev, Production depends on Staging — so it's a straight chain and a failure anywhere stops anything further downstream from running. The part that trips people up the first time they do this is realizing the manual approval for Production isn't something you write in this YAML file at all — it lives on the `production` environment object itself, configured under Approvals and Checks in the Azure DevOps project settings. So this pipeline file looks structurally identical for Dev, Staging, and Production — same deployment job shape — and the actual behavioral difference, 'this one needs a human to click approve,' comes entirely from environment-level configuration outside this file. That's actually a feature once you get used to it: whoever owns environment security can tighten or loosen the approval policy on production without anyone touching pipeline code or opening a PR. But it does mean if someone asks me 'where's the approval gate in this YAML,' the honest answer is 'it's not in here, go look at the environment's settings' — and that's worth saying out loud in an interview, because assuming it's all expressible in the pipeline file itself is a common and reasonable-sounding mistake.
questions.example: A failed Dev deployment stops Staging and Production from running at all (due to dependsOn chaining); a successful run through Staging pauses at Production until someone with approval rights on the `production` environment clicks Approve.
commonMistakes: Writing the approval gate as pipeline YAML logic instead of recognizing it's configured on the environment resource
Omitting dependsOn, allowing stages to run in parallel rather than the required sequence
Not distinguishing automatic promotion (no approval configured) from gated promotion (approval configured) per environment
Assuming the pipeline author alone controls the approval policy without environment-level permissions
keyPoints: dependsOn chains stages in the required Dev -> Staging -> Production sequence
Each stage deploys to a distinct, named Azure DevOps environment
Manual approval for Production is configured on the environment resource, not written in pipeline YAML
Separating sequencing (YAML) from gating policy (environment settings) allows independent ownership

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct three-stage structure with proper dependsOn sequencing
Correctly targets distinct named environments per stage
Correctly explains that the approval gate lives on the environment resource, not in YAML
Clear, accurate explanation of automatic vs. gated promotion behavior

questions.title: Writing a PromQL p95 Latency Query and Alert Rule
questions.prompt: Given a histogram metric `http_request_duration_seconds_bucket`, write a PromQL query for the 95th percentile request latency over a 5-minute window, and write a Prometheus alerting rule that fires if that p95 exceeds 0.5 seconds for 10 minutes straight.
questions.code:
# p95 latency query
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))

# alert rule
groups:
  - name: latency-alerts
    rules:
      - alert: HighP95Latency
        expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)) > 0.5
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "p95 latency above 500ms for 10+ minutes"
questions.modelAnswer: `histogram_quantile()` estimates a quantile from Prometheus's native histogram bucket counts (the `le` label on each bucket series represents 'less than or equal to' a given bucket boundary). It requires the bucket counts to first be converted to a per-second rate with `rate(...[5m])`, since the underlying `_bucket` series are cumulative counters, and summed across all instances/series `by (le)` so the quantile is computed over the aggregate distribution across all scraped targets rather than one quantile per instance (which would not correctly represent an overall 'p95 across the fleet'). The alert rule's `expr` reuses that same query, comparing it against the 0.5-second threshold; the `for: 10m` clause requires the condition to remain true continuously for 10 minutes before the alert actually fires (moving from Pending to Firing state), which deliberately avoids alerting on a brief, self-resolving latency blip and instead signals a sustained degradation worth waking someone up for.
questions.professionalAnswer: `histogram_quantile` is the function that turns Prometheus's bucketed histogram data into an actual percentile estimate — it leans on the `le` label, which marks each bucket as 'count of requests that took less than or equal to this duration.' Before you can hand that to `histogram_quantile`, you need `rate()` on the raw `_bucket` series first, because those are cumulative counters, not instantaneous values, and you sum `by (le)` so you're computing one p95 across the whole fleet's traffic, not one p95 per pod that you'd then have to somehow average together — averaging percentiles across instances doesn't give you a meaningful fleet-wide percentile, so this aggregate-then-quantile order matters. For the alert, I reuse that exact same expression and just compare it to 0.5s. The `for: 10m` is doing real work here too — without it, the alert would fire the instant the metric crosses the line even for one evaluation cycle, and you'd get paged for a 30-second blip that resolved itself before anyone even looked. Requiring it to stay above threshold continuously for 10 minutes is what turns this into a signal worth an on-call page instead of noise.
questions.example: If p95 latency spikes to 0.7s for 2 minutes and drops back to 0.3s, the alert never fires (condition wasn't sustained for the full 10m); if it stays above 0.5s continuously for 10+ minutes, it transitions from Pending to Firing.
commonMistakes: Applying histogram_quantile directly to raw bucket counters without rate() first
Computing a per-instance quantile and trying to average those instead of summing by (le) across the fleet first
Omitting the for: clause, causing the alert to fire on brief, self-resolving spikes
Confusing the le label's meaning or omitting it from the by() aggregation entirely
keyPoints: histogram_quantile requires rate() on the cumulative bucket counters first
Aggregation (sum by (le)) must happen before computing the quantile, not after
The for: duration prevents alerting on brief, non-sustained threshold breaches
The alert expression should reuse the same correctly-constructed query as the dashboard metric

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct p95 PromQL query using rate() and histogram_quantile() with sum by (le)
Correct alert rule with the 0.5s threshold and for: 10m duration
Correctly explains why rate() and aggregation order matter
Correctly explains the purpose of the for: clause

questions.title: Writing a NetworkPolicy to Isolate a Namespace
questions.prompt: Write a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy for the `payments` namespace so that pods labeled `app: payments-api` only accept inbound traffic on port 8443 from pods labeled `app: gateway` in the `edge` namespace, and reject all other inbound traffic.
questions.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: payments-api-ingress
  namespace: payments
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payments-api
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: edge
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: gateway
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8443
questions.modelAnswer: The `podSelector` scopes the policy to pods labeled `app: payments-api` within the `payments` namespace (NetworkPolicies are always namespace-scoped to where they're created). `policyTypes: [Ingress]` means this policy governs inbound traffic to the selected pods; because any NetworkPolicy selecting a pod switches that pod from 'allow all' to 'deny all except what's explicitly allowed' for the policy types it declares, simply creating this policy with one `ingress` rule automatically rejects everything not matching that rule — there's no need for a separate explicit deny rule. The single `ingress.from` entry combines both a `namespaceSelector` (matching the `edge` namespace via its automatically-applied `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` label) and a `podSelector` (matching `app: gateway`) within the same `from` list item, which Kubernetes interprets as an AND — traffic must come from a pod matching both selectors simultaneously, not from any pod in the edge namespace OR any gateway-labeled pod anywhere. The `ports` restriction further limits allowed traffic to TCP port 8443 specifically, so even a correctly-sourced gateway pod can't reach payments-api on any other port.
questions.professionalAnswer: podSelector picks out which pods this policy actually applies to — `app: payments-api` inside the `payments` namespace, since that's where I'm creating this resource. The important mechanic to get right here: the moment any NetworkPolicy selects a pod for Ingress, that pod flips from 'no restrictions, accept anything' to 'deny everything except what I explicitly allow' — so I don't need to write a separate 'deny all else' rule, that's just what happens by default once this policy exists and selects that pod. The trickiest part of writing this correctly is the single `from` entry combining a namespaceSelector and a podSelector in the same list item — that's an AND, meaning 'must be a gateway pod, AND must be in the edge namespace,' both at once. If I'd put the namespaceSelector and podSelector as two separate items in the `from` list instead of combined in one, that would've been an OR — 'anything in edge namespace, OR any pod anywhere labeled gateway' — which is a much looser and wrong policy for what was actually asked. And finally I lock it to port 8443 specifically, so even the correctly-matched gateway pod can't just talk to payments-api on some other port it happens to have open.
questions.example: A pod labeled app: gateway in namespace `staging` (not `edge`) attempting to reach payments-api is rejected, because it fails the namespaceSelector half of the AND condition even though it matches the podSelector.
commonMistakes: Putting namespaceSelector and podSelector as separate list items in `from`, turning the intended AND into an OR
Forgetting that selecting a pod for Ingress automatically denies unlisted traffic, and adding an unnecessary explicit deny rule
Omitting the ports restriction, allowing the correctly-sourced pod to reach any port
Using a namespace label other than the automatically-applied kubernetes.io/metadata.name without first manually labeling the namespace
keyPoints: podSelector scopes which pods the policy governs; policyTypes declares Ingress/Egress
Any policy selecting a pod implicitly denies unlisted traffic for the declared policy types
Combining namespaceSelector and podSelector in one `from` entry is an AND; separate entries are an OR
Port restriction further narrows allowed traffic beyond just source matching

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct podSelector scoping the policy to payments-api in the payments namespace
Correctly combines namespaceSelector and podSelector as an AND within one from entry
Correct port restriction to TCP 8443
Correctly explains the implicit deny-by-default behavior once a policy selects a pod

questions.title: Writing Helm Values Overrides for Multi-Environment Deployment
questions.prompt: A Helm chart's `values.yaml` defines a default of `replicaCount: 2`, `resources.requests.cpu: 100m`, and `ingress.enabled: false`. Write a `values-prod.yaml` override file that raises replicaCount to 6, raises the CPU request to 500m, and enables ingress with host `payments.ltvacademy.com` — and show the `helm upgrade` command that applies it correctly without losing the chart's other defaults.
questions.code:
# values-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 6

resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 500m

ingress:
  enabled: true
  host: payments.ltvacademy.com
questions.modelAnswer: A values override file only needs to specify the keys being changed; Helm merges the override file on top of the chart's default `values.yaml` rather than replacing it entirely, so unspecified defaults (like `resources.requests.memory` or `resources.limits`, if defined elsewhere in the default values) remain intact. The command `helm upgrade payments-api ./payments-api-chart -f values-prod.yaml` (or `-f values.yaml -f values-prod.yaml` if layering an explicit base file too) applies the override on top of the release currently deployed, using `-f` (or `--values`) rather than `--set`, which is more appropriate for multiple related overrides checked into version control.
