A critical detail: because YAML maps merge key-by-key but Helm's default merge behavior for nested maps is a deep merge (not a full replace) for most charts, specifying only `resources.requests.cpu` in the override does not require also restating `resources.requests.memory` if that key exists elsewhere in the base values — only the specifically listed keys are overridden; sibling keys not mentioned in the override are preserved from the base file.
questions.professionalAnswer: The override file only needs the keys that are actually changing — I'm not rewriting the whole values.yaml, just replicaCount, the one resource field, and the ingress block. Helm merges this on top of the chart's defaults rather than replacing the whole values set, so anything I don't mention here — memory requests, whatever else lives in the default values.yaml — stays exactly as the chart author set it. To apply it: `helm upgrade payments-api ./payments-api-chart -f values-prod.yaml`. I'd use `-f` here rather than a pile of `--set` flags, because this is the kind of override set that should live in version control and be reviewable in a PR, not typed inline on a deploy command where nobody can diff it later. One thing worth saying explicitly since it trips people up: the merge is a deep merge on the nested maps, so setting just `resources.requests.cpu` here doesn't nuke the rest of the `resources` block from the defaults — only the specific keys I actually wrote get overridden, and everything else under `resources` that I didn't touch is preserved from the base chart.
questions.example: If the chart's default values.yaml also sets `resources.requests.memory: 128Mi`, that value survives untouched after this override is applied, because the override only specifies `resources.requests.cpu`.
commonMistakes: Rewriting the entire values.yaml in the override file instead of only the changed keys
Using --set for a large, reviewable set of overrides instead of a version-controlled -f file
Assuming the override fully replaces a nested map (like resources) instead of deep-merging it
Forgetting to actually pass the override file to helm upgrade, leaving the release on old values
keyPoints: Override files should specify only the keys that differ from defaults
Helm deep-merges override values on top of chart defaults rather than replacing the whole set
-f/--values is preferable to --set for reviewable, version-controlled override sets
helm upgrade must explicitly reference the override file to take effect

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, minimal values-prod.yaml containing only the changed keys
Correct helm upgrade command referencing the override file
Correctly explains Helm's deep-merge behavior preserving unspecified defaults
Reasonable justification for -f over --set in this context

questions.title: Mounting a Key Vault Secret Into a Pod via Secrets Store CSI Driver
questions.prompt: Write the SecretProviderClass and the relevant Pod volume/volumeMount snippet needed so a Pod can mount a secret named `db-password` from an Azure Key Vault as a file, without storing the secret value in a Kubernetes Secret object.
questions.code:
apiVersion: secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io/v1
kind: SecretProviderClass
metadata:
  name: payments-kv-secrets
  namespace: payments
spec:
  provider: azure
  parameters:
    usePodIdentity: "false"
    useVMManagedIdentity: "false"
    clientID: "<workload-identity-client-id>"
    keyvaultName: "kv-payments-prod"
    tenantId: "<azure-tenant-id>"
    objects: |
      array:
        - |
          objectName: db-password
          objectType: secret
---
# Pod snippet
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: kv-secrets
      csi:
        driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io
        readOnly: true
        volumeAttributes:
          secretProviderClass: payments-kv-secrets
  containers:
    - name: app
      volumeMounts:
        - name: kv-secrets
          mountPath: /mnt/secrets
          readOnly: true
questions.modelAnswer: The SecretProviderClass declares which cloud provider's secret store to use (`azure`), the specific Key Vault (`keyvaultName`), and the list of objects to fetch (`db-password` as a `secret` type), along with the identity (`clientID`/`tenantId`) used to authenticate to Key Vault — ideally a federated workload identity rather than a static credential. The Pod references this SecretProviderClass through a CSI volume (`driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io`) rather than a standard Kubernetes `secret` volume type, and the CSI driver fetches the secret value directly from Key Vault at pod startup, presenting it to the container as a file under the mount path — the secret value is never persisted as a Kubernetes Secret object (and therefore never stored, even base64-encoded, in etcd) unless the optional secret-sync feature is explicitly enabled. This is the key security property being asked for: the value only exists in the Pod's mounted volume (typically backed by tmpfs) and is fetched fresh from Key Vault, rather than being copied into and persisted by the Kubernetes API's own secret storage.
questions.professionalAnswer: The SecretProviderClass is basically the configuration object that says 'here's which Key Vault, here's which secret inside it, here's the identity to use to authenticate.' The identity part matters a lot — I'd want that to be a federated workload identity, not some static client secret sitting elsewhere, otherwise I've just moved the 'long-lived credential problem' one level over instead of solving it. The Pod side is where the actual property people usually care about shows up: instead of a normal Kubernetes Secret volume, this uses a CSI volume pointing at the secrets-store driver, referencing that SecretProviderClass by name. What that buys you is the secret value gets fetched live from Key Vault and handed to the container as a file on a mounted volume — it never gets written into a Kubernetes Secret object, which means it's never sitting base64-'encoded'-but-not-encrypted in etcd waiting for someone with cluster access to `kubectl get secret -o yaml` it. If someone specifically asks 'why not just use a regular Secret synced from Key Vault,' the honest answer is: that's also an option (the CSI driver supports secret-sync), but it reintroduces the exact risk — a copy of the secret now persisted inside the cluster — that mounting it directly via CSI avoids.
questions.example: An operator with read access to Secrets in the payments namespace cannot retrieve db-password via `kubectl get secret`, because no Secret object was ever created — the value only ever existed as a file inside the Pod's own mounted volume, sourced live from Key Vault.
commonMistakes: Using a standard Kubernetes Secret volume instead of the CSI driver, which requires the value to be stored as a Secret object
Authenticating to Key Vault with a static client secret instead of federated workload identity
Not realizing the optional secret-sync feature would reintroduce the exact persisted-Secret risk being avoided
Omitting readOnly: true on the volume/mount, unnecessarily allowing writes to the secret mount
keyPoints: SecretProviderClass declares the provider, vault, objects to fetch, and authentication identity
The CSI volume type (not a standard Secret volume) fetches the value live without persisting it as a Kubernetes Secret
This avoids the secret ever being stored, even base64-encoded, in etcd
Authentication should use federated workload identity rather than a static credential

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct SecretProviderClass referencing the right provider, vault, and object
Correct Pod CSI volume and volumeMount configuration
Correctly explains that the secret is never persisted as a Kubernetes Secret object
Notes the preference for federated workload identity over a static credential

questions.title: Provisioning an AKS Cluster With a Dedicated Node Pool in Terraform
questions.prompt: Write Terraform resource blocks to provision an AKS cluster with a default system node pool of 2 nodes, plus a separate user node pool named `workloads` that autoscales between 2 and 8 nodes using `Standard_D4s_v5` VMs.
questions.modelAnswer: The `default_node_pool` block inside `azurerm_kubernetes_cluster` is required by the provider and typically hosts system/critical workloads (it cannot be deleted without recreating the cluster, which is why most real deployments keep it small and dedicated to system pods via taints, and run application workloads on separate pools). The separate `azurerm_kubernetes_cluster_node_pool` resource adds the `workloads` pool independently, referencing the cluster via `kubernetes_cluster_id` rather than being nested in the cluster resource — this is deliberate in the provider's design, since additional node pools can be created, resized, or destroyed without touching the cluster resource itself, reducing the blast radius of changes. `enable_auto_scaling = true` with `min_count`/`max_count` delegates scaling decisions to the Cluster Autoscaler add-on rather than a fixed `node_count`; when autoscaling is enabled, Terraform should generally avoid fighting the autoscaler over the live node count on subsequent applies (some setups use `ignore_changes` on `node_count` for this reason), since the autoscaler will adjust it at runtime independently of what's declared in code.
questions.professionalAnswer: The default_node_pool inside the cluster resource is mandatory — AKS won't let you create a cluster without one — and in practice I treat it as the system pool: small, stable, meant for AKS's own system pods, and I keep application workloads off it on purpose. The workloads pool is its own separate resource type, `azurerm_kubernetes_cluster_node_pool`, linked to the cluster by ID rather than nested inside it — and that separation is actually convenient, because it means I can resize, retag, or even destroy and recreate that one pool without touching the cluster resource at all, which keeps the blast radius of any one change small. For the autoscaling piece, `enable_auto_scaling = true` with min/max count 2 to 8 hands control over to the Cluster Autoscaler at runtime — and here's the gotcha worth mentioning: once that's live, the actual node_count the autoscaler settles on will drift from whatever I declared in Terraform, because the autoscaler is adjusting it live based on load. If I don't account for that, every subsequent `terraform plan` shows a 'change' on node_count that isn't really a change I made — it's just the autoscaler doing its job — so teams often add `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [node_count] }` on an autoscaled pool specifically to stop Terraform from fighting the autoscaler.
questions.example: After autoscaling kicks the workloads pool up to 6 nodes under load, a subsequent `terraform plan` without ignore_changes on node_count would show a planned change back down to 2 — fighting the very autoscaler the configuration just enabled.
commonMistakes: Putting application workloads on the default/system node pool instead of a dedicated pool
Nesting the second node pool inside the cluster resource instead of using the separate resource type
Not accounting for node_count drift once autoscaling is enabled, causing Terraform to fight the autoscaler
Omitting min_count/max_count or enable_auto_scaling, leaving the pool at a fixed size despite the requirement
keyPoints: default_node_pool is mandatory and conventionally reserved for system workloads
Additional node pools use a separate resource type for independent lifecycle management
enable_auto_scaling with min/max delegates scaling to Cluster Autoscaler at runtime
node_count drift from live autoscaling should be handled (e.g., ignore_changes) to avoid Terraform fighting the autoscaler

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct AKS cluster resource with a 2-node default/system pool
Correct separate node pool resource named workloads with correct VM size
Correctly configures autoscaling with min_count 2 / max_count 8
Explains the node_count drift issue once autoscaling is enabled

questions.title: Gating a Pipeline on a Container Image Vulnerability Scan
questions.prompt: Write a GitHub Actions step (using Trivy) that scans a freshly built container image and fails the pipeline if any CRITICAL or HIGH severity vulnerabilities with an available fix are found, while not failing the build on vulnerabilities with no fix available yet.
questions.code:
- name: Scan image with Trivy
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.24.0
  with:
    image-ref: "myrepo/payments-api:${{ github.sha }}"
    severity: "CRITICAL,HIGH"
    ignore-unfixed: true
    exit-code: "1"
    format: "table"
questions.modelAnswer: `severity: "CRITICAL,HIGH"` scopes the scan's pass/fail decision to only those two severity levels, so lower-severity findings (MEDIUM/LOW) are reported but don't by themselves fail the build. `ignore-unfixed: true` is the key setting for the stated requirement: it excludes vulnerabilities for which no patched version currently exists from the exit-code calculation, which matters because failing a build on an unfixable vulnerability accomplishes nothing operationally — there's no remediation action the team can take to pass the gate, so the gate would just become a permanent, un-actionable blocker that teams eventually learn to ignore or bypass entirely, undermining the gate's credibility for genuinely actionable findings. `exit-code: "1"` is what actually causes the GitHub Actions step (and therefore the job) to fail when matching vulnerabilities are found; without explicitly setting a non-zero exit code, some scanner actions default to reporting without failing the pipeline, which would make the 'gate' purely informational rather than enforced.
questions.professionalAnswer: `severity: CRITICAL,HIGH` keeps the actual gate — the thing that can fail the build — scoped to just those two levels; medium and low still show up in the report, I'm just not blocking a deploy over them. The setting that's really doing the specific work asked for here is `ignore-unfixed: true`. Without it, you'd fail a build over a CVE in some base image package that genuinely has no patch released yet — and that's a bad gate, because there's nothing the engineer can actually do about it. A security gate that blocks you with no path to green just trains people to find workarounds — skip the scan, override the gate, whatever — and once that habit forms it undermines the gate for the vulnerabilities that actually are fixable, which is the whole point of having it. `exit-code: "1"` is the part I'd double check isn't missing, because some scanning actions will happily run, print a nice report, and exit 0 regardless of findings unless you explicitly tell them to fail the job — and a scan step that can never fail the pipeline isn't a gate, it's just a report nobody's required to read.
questions.example: A HIGH-severity CVE with a patched version available fails the build (actionable, exit-code triggers failure); a CRITICAL CVE in a base image with no fix yet released is reported but does not fail the build, thanks to ignore-unfixed.
commonMistakes: Omitting ignore-unfixed, which blocks builds on un-actionable vulnerabilities and erodes trust in the gate
Not setting an explicit non-zero exit code, leaving the scan purely informational rather than enforced
Scoping severity too broadly (including LOW/MEDIUM in the failing criteria) and generating excessive noise
Scanning the wrong image reference (e.g., a cached/previous tag) instead of the freshly built image
keyPoints: severity scope should match the actual risk tolerance for blocking a build
ignore-unfixed avoids blocking on vulnerabilities with no available remediation
An explicit non-zero exit code is required to make the scan actually enforceable, not just informational
The gate's credibility depends on only blocking on genuinely actionable findings

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly scopes severity to CRITICAL and HIGH
Correctly sets ignore-unfixed to exclude un-actionable findings
Correctly ensures the step fails the pipeline via explicit exit code
Explains why gating on unfixable vulnerabilities undermines the gate's credibility

questions.title: Writing a Namespace-Scoped RBAC Role and RoleBinding
questions.prompt: A CI service account named `deployer` in namespace `payments` needs to be able to create, update, and delete Deployments and Services in that namespace only — nothing cluster-wide, and no access to Secrets. Write the Role and RoleBinding.
questions.code:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: deployer-role
  namespace: payments
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["create", "update", "patch", "delete", "get", "list"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["services"]
    verbs: ["create", "update", "patch", "delete", "get", "list"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: deployer-binding
  namespace: payments
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: deployer
    namespace: payments
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: deployer-role
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
questions.modelAnswer: A `Role` (not `ClusterRole`) is scoped to the namespace declared in its `metadata.namespace`, which is the correct choice here since the requirement is explicitly namespace-only access; a `ClusterRole` would grant the permission across every namespace in the cluster regardless of how it's bound, which would violate the 'nothing cluster-wide' requirement even if bound via a RoleBinding in one namespace. The `rules` list scopes to the `apps` API group for Deployments and the core (`""`) API group for Services, with verbs covering create/update/patch/delete plus get/list (practically necessary for a CI tool to check current state before applying changes) — critically, no rule grants any verb on `secrets`, satisfying the explicit exclusion. The `RoleBinding` binds the `deployer` ServiceAccount (itself scoped to the `payments` namespace) to this namespace-scoped Role, which means the resulting permissions apply only within `payments` — using a ClusterRoleBinding here, even referencing this same Role indirectly, is not how RoleBindings work (a RoleBinding can only reference a Role in the same namespace or a ClusterRole, and either way a RoleBinding's grant is always scoped to its own namespace).
questions.professionalAnswer: Role over ClusterRole is the first decision that matters here, because the requirement is explicit — namespace only, nothing cluster-wide — and a ClusterRole, even if I only bind it inside one namespace with a RoleBinding, still represents a cluster-scoped permission object that's easy to accidentally reuse somewhere broader later. A plain Role scoped by its own namespace field just can't do that, which is the safer default when the requirement says 'this namespace, and only this namespace.' For the rules, I included get/list alongside the write verbs even though the prompt didn't explicitly ask for them, because in practice a CI deploy tool almost always needs to check the current state of a Deployment before patching it — a write-only role without read access tends to just break in practice the first time the tool tries to do a diff. And I was careful to leave Secrets out entirely — no apiGroup/resource rule touches secrets, which directly satisfies 'no access to Secrets,' and it's worth saying out loud in review, because 'no rule granting X' is genuinely how you express 'deny X' in RBAC — there's no explicit deny syntax, access is purely additive, so omission is the mechanism.
questions.example: Attempting `kubectl get secrets -n payments` as the deployer service account is denied, because no rule in the Role grants any verb on the secrets resource — RBAC is purely additive, so omission acts as denial.
commonMistakes: Using ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding instead of namespace-scoped Role/RoleBinding, violating the namespace-only requirement
Granting access to Secrets inadvertently via a wildcard resource rule
Omitting get/list verbs, leaving a CI tool unable to check current state before applying changes
Not understanding that RBAC is purely additive — there's no explicit deny, only omission
keyPoints: Role (not ClusterRole) correctly scopes permissions to the single namespace
Rules grant only Deployments and Services, explicitly excluding Secrets by omission
RoleBinding correctly binds the namespace-scoped ServiceAccount to the namespace-scoped Role
RBAC is additive-only; excluding a resource means simply not granting any verb on it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses namespace-scoped Role rather than ClusterRole
Correctly scopes rules to Deployments and Services only, excluding Secrets
Correct RoleBinding linking the ServiceAccount to the Role within the namespace
Correctly explains RBAC's additive-only nature as the exclusion mechanism

questions.title: Pods CrashLoopBackOff After a Deployment With Tight Memory Limits
questions.prompt: After rolling out a new version of a service, several pods show `CrashLoopBackOff`. `kubectl describe pod` shows 'Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled' with restart count climbing. CPU usage looks normal. Walk through your diagnosis and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: OOMKilled means the container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel's cgroup controller killed it — this is unrelated to CPU, which explains why CPU metrics look normal. The diagnosis sequence: first confirm the actual memory limit set on the container (`kubectl describe pod` or the Deployment's resources.limits.memory) and compare it against what the new version's actual memory footprint looks like, ideally pulled from metrics (kubectl top pod, or historical data in Prometheus/Container Insights if available) from before the crash. Common root causes to check: the new release genuinely increased memory usage (a new dependency, a cache, a memory leak under certain inputs) without the limit being raised to match; or the limit was copied from the old version's profile and never revisited. If metrics show usage climbing steadily rather than spiking once, that points to a leak in the new code rather than a simple undersized limit, which needs a code-level fix, not just a higher limit — raising the limit on a genuine leak only delays the crash and risks destabilizing the node when it does happen. If usage is simply higher but stable, raising `resources.limits.memory` (and correspondingly `requests.memory`, since requests should generally scale with expected real usage) resolves it. The fix should be validated by watching actual memory usage under load post-fix, not just confirming the CrashLoopBackOff stops, since a limit set just barely above the new steady-state is fragile.
questions.professionalAnswer: OOMKilled is memory, full stop — the cgroup killed the container for going over its memory limit, which is exactly why CPU looks fine; those are two completely separate mechanisms. First thing I check is what the limit actually is versus what this new version is actually using — kubectl top pod if I can catch it running, or whatever historical memory graph I've got for this service. Then the real branch point: is usage just higher-but-stable than before, or is it climbing the whole time the pod's alive? If it's climbing steadily until it hits the ceiling, that smells like a leak in whatever changed in this release, and bumping the memory limit doesn't fix that — it just buys a little more time before the same crash happens, and now it might take out something else on the node when it does. If it's stable but genuinely higher — say the new version added a cache or a new library with a bigger baseline footprint — then yes, raise the limit to actually match reality, and raise requests too since that's supposed to track real expected usage, not just be a number copied from six versions ago. Either way, I wouldn't call it fixed just because CrashLoopBackOff stopped — I'd want to watch it under real load for a while afterward, because a limit set right at the edge of the new steady state is just setting up the next version of this same incident.
questions.example: Memory usage graph shows a steady climb from 150Mi to the 256Mi limit over 40 minutes post-deploy, then OOMKill and restart, repeating — this pattern (steady climb to ceiling, not a spike) points to a leak introduced in the new release, not simply an undersized limit.
commonMistakes: Treating every OOMKilled as 'just raise the limit' without checking whether usage is leaking versus simply higher
Confusing OOMKilled with a CPU-related issue since the symptom is a crash loop
Raising the memory limit without also reconsidering the memory request
Declaring the incident resolved once the crash loop stops, without validating stability under real load afterward
keyPoints: OOMKilled is a memory cgroup kill, unrelated to CPU usage or throttling
Distinguishes a steady climb (likely leak, needs code fix) from a stable-but-higher footprint (needs a limit increase)
Memory requests should be reconsidered alongside any limit change
Fix should be validated under real load, not just by the crash loop stopping

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies OOMKilled as a memory-limit cgroup kill, unrelated to CPU
Correctly distinguishes a leak (climbing usage) from a simple undersized limit (stable higher usage)
Proposes the correct fix for each case (code fix vs. limit/request increase)
Validates the fix under real load rather than assuming success from the crash loop stopping

questions.title: Rolling Update Stuck With New Pods Never Becoming Ready
questions.prompt: A rollout is stuck: new-version pods are Running but never show as Ready, old pods are being kept alive, and `kubectl rollout status` just hangs. How do you investigate and what are the likely root causes?
questions.modelAnswer: A rollout stalls exactly like this when new pods are Running (the container process started) but failing their readiness probe, since Kubernetes won't proceed terminating old pods or consider the rollout progressing until new pods pass readiness — this is actually the rollout mechanism working as designed to protect availability, not a bug. The investigation sequence: `kubectl describe pod <new-pod>` to see recent Events, specifically readiness probe failure messages (e.g., 'Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503' or a connection refused/timeout); then check the probe's actual configuration (path, port, initialDelaySeconds, timeoutSeconds) against what the new version's container actually does at startup — a very common cause is the new version takes longer to become genuinely ready (e.g., a larger cache warm-up, a new startup dependency check) than `initialDelaySeconds` allows for, so the probe starts checking before the app can possibly respond successfully. Another common cause is the readiness endpoint itself changed or broke in the new version (a new dependency check added to the health endpoint that's failing, like a downstream service the health check now pings but can't reach in this environment). Checking application logs for the new pod (`kubectl logs`) alongside the probe failure reason narrows it to an app-level startup problem versus a probe-configuration mismatch. The fix is either adjusting probe timing/configuration to match real startup behavior, or fixing whatever the readiness endpoint is actually failing to verify.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is actually the rollout behaving correctly, just stuck on a real problem — Kubernetes won't tear down old pods until new ones pass readiness, which is exactly the safety mechanism you want, it's just surfacing that something's wrong with the new version rather than silently replacing good pods with broken ones. First move is `kubectl describe pod` on one of the new pods and read the Events at the bottom — it'll usually say exactly why readiness is failing, something like a timeout or a non-200 from the probe's endpoint. From there it's basically two buckets: either the probe timing is wrong for this version — the app genuinely needs longer to warm up than `initialDelaySeconds` gives it credit for, which I've seen happen a lot when someone adds a bigger cache load or a new startup check and nobody revisited the probe settings — or the readiness endpoint itself is broken in this version, which I'd confirm by just looking at the app logs for that pod, not just the probe failure message. If the logs show the health endpoint is pinging some downstream dependency that isn't reachable in this environment, that's an app bug or a missing config, not a probe-timing issue, and bumping initialDelaySeconds would just mask it until it times out anyway.
questions.example: Describe Pod Events show: 'Readiness probe failed: Get "http://10.1.2.3:8080/health": dial tcp 10.1.2.3:8080: connect: connection refused' repeated for several minutes past initialDelaySeconds=10 — pointing to the app genuinely not listening yet, not a transient blip.
commonMistakes: Assuming the rollout is 'broken' rather than correctly blocking on a genuine readiness failure
Not checking kubectl describe pod Events for the specific readiness failure reason
Only adjusting probe timing without checking whether the readiness endpoint itself is actually broken
Confusing liveness probe failures (causes restarts) with readiness probe failures (blocks traffic/rollout progress) when reading symptoms
keyPoints: A stuck rollout with Running-but-not-Ready new pods reflects correct safety behavior, not a bug
kubectl describe pod Events usually name the specific readiness failure reason
Root cause is either probe timing mismatched to real startup time, or a genuinely broken readiness endpoint
Application logs, not just the probe failure message, are needed to distinguish the two

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why the rollout is safely blocked rather than broken
Describes a concrete, correct investigation sequence (describe pod, logs)
Correctly identifies both probe-timing and broken-endpoint as plausible root causes
Proposes an appropriate fix matched to the actual root cause

questions.title: HPA Not Scaling Despite High CPU Load
questions.prompt: Users report slow response times. `kubectl top pod` shows CPU usage well above what should trigger scaling, but `kubectl get hpa` shows the replica count unchanged for the last 20 minutes and TARGETS showing `<unknown>/60%`. What's going on and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: `<unknown>` in the HPA's TARGETS column means the HPA controller cannot retrieve the metric it needs at all, which is a different and more fundamental problem than 'scaling too slowly' — the HPA isn't making a bad scaling decision, it's making no decision because it has no data. The most common cause is the metrics-server (or a custom metrics adapter, for custom/external metrics) being unavailable, misconfigured, or unable to reach the target pods — check `kubectl get apiservices | grep metrics` and `kubectl -n kube-system logs` on metrics-server for connection errors. A second very common cause, often overlooked because it produces the exact same `<unknown>` symptom: the target Deployment's containers have no `resources.requests.cpu` set at all, and HPA's CPU utilization percentage calculation is defined relative to requests — without a request value to divide by, the percentage is undefined, so the HPA reports unknown rather than guessing. The fix path is: first confirm metrics-server is healthy and actually returning data for these pods (`kubectl top pod` working at all is a good sign metrics-server itself is fine, which shifts suspicion toward the second cause); then check the Deployment's resources.requests.cpu — if it's missing, the real fix is adding a sensible CPU request, after which the HPA should start reporting a real percentage and begin scaling normally.
questions.professionalAnswer: `<unknown>` is the detail that changes the whole diagnosis here — this isn't 'HPA is slow to react,' it's 'HPA literally has no number to react to.' Since kubectl top pod is working, metrics-server itself is basically proven healthy — if it weren't, top pod would fail too. So I'd go straight to the Deployment's resource requests, because this is the classic way to get exactly this symptom: HPA's percentage math is current-usage divided by requested-CPU, and if there's no CPU request set on the container at all, there's nothing to divide by, so it reports unknown instead of making up a number. I've seen this exact ticket before — someone deploys a new service, forgets to set resources.requests.cpu, HPA is configured and looks fine in the manifest, but it just sits there forever showing unknown because it mathematically can't compute a percentage. The fix is adding a real CPU request that reflects actual typical usage, and once that's in place the HPA starts reporting an actual percentage on the next reconcile and scales normally from there — no change to the HPA object itself needed, the problem was always upstream of it.
questions.example: `kubectl describe deployment` shows no `resources` block at all on the container; adding `resources.requests.cpu: 250m` resolves the `<unknown>` reading within one HPA reconcile cycle and scaling resumes.
commonMistakes: Assuming <unknown> means the same thing as 'scaling too slowly' and focusing on HPA tuning parameters instead
Not checking whether the target workload has resources.requests.cpu set at all
Jumping straight to metrics-server troubleshooting without first checking whether kubectl top pod itself works (a quick signal metrics-server is healthy)
Fixing the symptom by manually scaling replicas instead of addressing why the HPA can't compute its own target
keyPoints: <unknown> means the HPA has no metric data at all, not that it's scaling too slowly
A missing resources.requests.cpu on the target workload is a common root cause of <unknown>, since utilization percentage is calculated against requests
kubectl top pod working is a useful signal that metrics-server itself is healthy
The fix is setting a correct CPU request on the target workload, not adjusting the HPA object

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interprets <unknown> as a missing-metric problem, not a slow-scaling problem
Correctly identifies missing resources.requests.cpu as the likely root cause
Describes a sound diagnostic sequence distinguishing metrics-server health from request misconfiguration
Proposes the correct, targeted fix

questions.title: Terraform State Out of Sync After a Partially Failed Apply
questions.prompt: A `terraform apply` failed partway through creating several resources due to a transient cloud API error. Some resources were created successfully before the failure; others were not. The next `terraform plan` shows confusing, seemingly wrong diffs. How do you recover safely?
questions.modelAnswer: A partial apply failure typically leaves state in one of two conditions: either Terraform successfully recorded the resources that were actually created before the failure (the common, well-behaved case, since Terraform writes state incrementally as each resource completes, not only at the very end), or in rarer cases a resource was created in the cloud provider but the state write for it didn't complete before the process died, leaving state unaware of a real, now-orphaned resource. The safe recovery sequence starts with `terraform plan`, read carefully: diffs showing Terraform wanting to create resources that plan output suggests already exist (e.g., a naming conflict error on the next apply) point to the second case — a real resource exists in the cloud but isn't in state. Confirm directly in the cloud provider's console/CLI whether each resource in question actually exists before taking any action, rather than trusting state alone. For resources confirmed to exist in the cloud but missing from state, `terraform import` brings them under management without recreating them; for resources state believes exist but the cloud confirms were never created, nothing special is needed — plan will correctly show them to be created on the next apply. Only after state accurately reflects cloud reality should `terraform apply` be re-run; naively re-running apply immediately after a partial failure, without first inspecting what's real, risks either duplicate-resource creation errors or Terraform attempting to manage a resource it doesn't know exists, producing further confusing errors.
questions.professionalAnswer: The good news with a partial failure is Terraform usually writes state incrementally as things succeed, not all at once at the end — so the typical case is state is actually accurate for what did get created, and the next plan is just correctly showing you the rest still needs to happen. But I never assume that's the case, because the other failure mode — a resource got created in the cloud, but the state write for it never landed before the process died — produces genuinely confusing plan output, usually a 'resource already exists' error on the next apply for something state thinks doesn't exist yet. So my first move is always to go check reality directly — Azure portal, az cli, whatever — for the specific resources the confusing diff is complaining about, rather than trusting either Terraform's state or my assumption about what probably happened. If I confirm something's really there but state doesn't know about it, `terraform import` brings it into state without touching the actual resource — no delete-and-recreate risk. If I confirm something genuinely isn't there despite what I expected, I don't need to do anything special, the next plan already has that right. The one thing I'd actively avoid is just rerunning apply blind the moment it fails — on a partial failure like this, that's a good way to either hit a duplicate-resource error mid-run again, or worse, have Terraform try to do something destructive based on a state that doesn't match reality.
questions.example: Plan shows Terraform wanting to create a storage account that apply's error log actually confirms was created moments before the transient failure — `terraform import azurerm_storage_account.this /subscriptions/.../storageAccounts/...` brings it into state correctly instead of attempting to recreate it and hitting a naming conflict.
commonMistakes: Assuming state is always accurate after a partial failure without verifying against the actual cloud provider
Immediately rerunning apply without first understanding what the confusing diff is actually telling you
Deleting and recreating a resource that already exists correctly, instead of importing it
Not recognizing that Terraform writes state incrementally, which is why most resources created before the failure are usually already tracked correctly
keyPoints: State is usually accurate for resources created before the failure, since Terraform writes state incrementally
Confusing diffs often indicate a real resource exists in the cloud but isn't recorded in state
Verify directly against the cloud provider before taking any recovery action
terraform import is the safe recovery path for real-but-untracked resources; blind reapply risks duplicate-creation errors

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the two possible post-failure state conditions
Describes verifying against actual cloud state before acting
Correctly proposes terraform import as the recovery mechanism for untracked real resources
Explicitly avoids the unsafe 'just rerun apply blind' approach

questions.title: Terraform Plan Shows Drift on Every Run
questions.prompt: Every time anyone runs `terraform plan` on a particular resource, it shows a diff wanting to change the same one or two attributes back to what's in the Terraform config — even immediately after a clean apply. Nothing in the code has changed. What's happening and how do you resolve it?
questions.modelAnswer: A diff that reappears on every plan immediately after a clean apply, with no code changes, is the signature of either real configuration drift being continuously reintroduced by something outside Terraform, or a provider/attribute quirk rather than genuine drift. First, check whether another process is actively modifying the resource outside Terraform — a common real-world cause is an auto-remediation policy (e.g., an Azure Policy with a 'modify' effect, or a security tool) silently reverting an attribute every time it runs, right after Terraform sets it, which looks exactly like perpetual drift because it is perpetual drift, just caused by a competing system rather than a human console change. Second, check whether the attribute in question is one the provider computes or normalizes differently than how it's expressed in config (e.g., a case-sensitivity difference, a default value the API applies server-side that doesn't exactly match what was written, or an attribute order/format difference) — this produces a 'fake' diff that isn't really drift at all, just a representation mismatch, and is usually a known provider quirk or bug with a documented workaround (often `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [...] }` for an attribute that's legitimately managed elsewhere, or upgrading the provider version if it's a bug that's since been fixed). The resolution differs by cause: for competing-system drift, either stop the competing system from touching that attribute or explicitly decide which system owns it (and use ignore_changes if the other system should win); for a provider quirk, ignore_changes or a provider upgrade is appropriate — but ignore_changes should never be applied reflexively without first confirming which of these two situations is actually occurring, since masking real externally-caused drift with ignore_changes can hide an actual security or compliance problem (an unauthorized change happening repeatedly).
questions.professionalAnswer: Perpetual drift right after a clean apply, with zero code changes, almost always means something outside Terraform is actively fighting it, or the provider itself is just reporting a cosmetic difference that isn't really drift. I've chased this exact pattern down to an Azure Policy with a 'modify' effect more than once — it reverts some tag or setting back to its own idea of compliant, Terraform sets it back on apply, policy reverts it again on its own schedule, and from the plan's perspective that looks like infinite drift, because functionally it is — just caused by policy, not a person clicking around in the portal. So step one is actually figure out who or what else might be touching this attribute, not assume it's a config bug. If it turns out nothing else is touching it, the other usual suspect is the provider itself reporting something in a slightly different shape than what's in the .tf file — a case difference, some default the API injects that isn't exactly what you wrote — which is a known category of provider quirk, sometimes a genuine bug fixed in a later provider version. I'd only reach for `lifecycle { ignore_changes }` once I actually know which of these two situations I'm in, because slapping ignore_changes on reflexively can quietly hide a real problem — if it's policy or some other system legitimately supposed to own that attribute, fine, ignore it deliberately. But if it's an unauthorized change happening on a schedule, ignore_changes just means Terraform stops telling you about it.
questions.example: An Azure Policy auto-tagging rule resets `tags.costCenter` to a policy-determined value every 24 hours; Terraform's config specifies a different value, producing identical drift on every plan — resolved by either aligning the Terraform value with policy or explicitly excluding that tag key via ignore_changes once the cause is confirmed.
commonMistakes: Assuming the drift is simply a Terraform or provider bug without checking for an external system actively reverting the attribute
Reflexively adding ignore_changes without first determining whether the drift reflects an unauthorized/unexpected external change
Not distinguishing real attribute drift from a cosmetic provider representation mismatch
Repeatedly reapplying as a 'fix' without investigating why the same diff keeps reappearing
keyPoints: Perpetual post-apply drift usually means either an external system is reverting the attribute, or it's a provider representation quirk
Diagnosis requires identifying which of these two causes is actually occurring before acting
ignore_changes is only an appropriate fix once the cause is understood, never as a reflexive first move
Masking externally-caused drift without understanding it can hide a real unauthorized-change problem

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies competing external systems as a plausible cause of perpetual drift
Correctly identifies provider representation quirks as an alternative cause
Describes a sound diagnostic approach to distinguish the two before acting
Flags the risk of reflexively masking real drift with ignore_changes

questions.title: GitHub Actions Builds Intermittently Fail With Corrupted Cache
questions.prompt: A CI workflow occasionally fails with dependency installation errors that look like corrupted or incomplete packages, but only intermittently — most runs succeed. Re-running the failed job usually fixes it. What's the likely cause and how do you address it properly rather than just re-running jobs?
questions.modelAnswer: Intermittent, re-run-fixes-it dependency failures are a classic symptom of a corrupted cache entry rather than a real dependency problem: if a previous job was interrupted (cancelled, timed out, or runner failure) partway through writing a cache entry, `actions/cache`'s save step can leave a partially-written or inconsistent cache saved under a valid-looking key, which later runs then restore and fail against, while runs that happen to save a clean cache (or hit a cold cache and install fresh) succeed. Re-running 'fixes' it only coincidentally, often because the re-run generates a fresh cache-miss-then-save cycle that happens to succeed, not because anything was actually diagnosed. The correct fix is not to make re-running easier or more automatic, but to make corruption impossible or quickly detectable: verify the install step uses a mechanism that validates integrity (most package managers verify checksums/lockfile hashes on install already, so a truly corrupted cache should usually be caught and fail loudly rather than silently installing bad packages — if it's silently succeeding with bad packages, that's a separate and more serious integrity-verification gap worth investigating); and more directly, invalidate and replace the specific suspect cache entry (bump a cache-key version suffix, or delete the cache via the GitHub UI/API) to force a clean rebuild, then monitor whether the intermittent failures recur. If they do recur with a fresh cache, the root cause is more likely a flaky network/registry issue during the original cache-populating install rather than cache corruption itself, which calls for retry logic in the install step rather than a cache fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: The pattern itself — intermittent, and a re-run fixes it — is the tell that this is almost certainly a cache issue, not a real dependency problem. What I think is actually happening: some earlier run got cancelled or timed out mid-way through saving its cache, and that left a partial or inconsistent cache entry sitting under a key that looks perfectly valid to later runs. Those later runs restore that bad cache and fail; runs that happen to get a cache miss and install fresh, or that saved a clean cache, succeed — hence 'intermittent.' Just re-running and moving on is treating the symptom, not the cause — the bad cache entry is still sitting there under that key, waiting to bite the next run that restores it. What I'd actually do is go kill that specific cache entry — either bump something in the cache key so it's forced to regenerate, or just delete it directly through the GitHub UI or API — and then watch closely over the next several runs. If the intermittent failures stop, that confirms it was the stale/corrupt cache and the fix holds. If they come back even with a fresh cache, I've learned something new — now it's more likely a flaky network blip hitting the package registry during install, which is a different problem needing retry logic in the install step itself, not a cache fix.
questions.example: A cancelled run leaves a cache entry partially written; subsequent runs restoring that exact key fail on install with checksum mismatches, while runs that happen to generate a fresh cache succeed — deleting the suspect cache entry resolves the intermittent failures going forward.
commonMistakes: Treating 're-running fixes it' as an acceptable permanent workaround instead of a diagnostic clue
Not considering that a cancelled/interrupted prior run could leave a corrupted cache entry under a valid key
Jumping to 'flaky network' as the cause without first ruling out (or confirming) cache corruption specifically
Fixing the symptom (auto-retry the job) without ever addressing or even identifying the actual root cause
keyPoints: Intermittent, re-run-fixes-it failures are a classic cache-corruption signature
A cancelled or interrupted job can leave a partially written cache entry under a valid-looking key
The fix is to invalidate/delete the specific suspect cache entry, not to make re-running routine
If failures persist after a cache reset, the real cause is more likely network/registry flakiness, needing retry logic instead

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies cache corruption from an interrupted prior run as the likely cause
Explains why re-running appears to fix it without actually addressing the root cause
Proposes invalidating/deleting the specific cache entry as the correct remedy
Identifies the correct follow-up diagnosis (network flakiness) if the fix doesn't hold

questions.title: Azure DevOps Release Blocked by a Service Connection Permission Error
questions.prompt: A release pipeline that deploys to a production environment suddenly starts failing at the deployment step with a permissions/authorization error, even though nothing in the pipeline YAML changed and the same pipeline deployed successfully yesterday. How do you investigate?
questions.modelAnswer: Since the pipeline definition itself is unchanged, the cause lives outside the YAML — most commonly in the service connection's underlying identity or the target resource's access policy, both of which can change independently of pipeline code and without any visible diff in the repository. The investigation should start by reading the actual error message carefully (Azure DevOps surfaces the underlying cloud provider's authorization error, e.g., an Azure RBAC 'does not have authorization to perform action' or an expired credential message), then check the service connection's health directly in Project Settings > Service Connections (there's usually a 'Verify' action) rather than assuming it's fine because it worked yesterday. Common root causes: the service principal or managed identity backing the service connection had its role assignment removed or scoped down (e.g., someone cleaning up 'unused' permissions, or a separate IaC change to IAM that inadvertently affected this identity); a client secret on the service principal expired (these often have fixed expiry dates set when created, silently approaching and then passing that date); or the target resource itself changed its access policy (e.g., a Key Vault access policy, a storage account firewall rule) independently of anything in this pipeline. Because the failure is at the authorization boundary rather than the pipeline logic, the fix is almost never a pipeline code change — it's restoring or rotating the credential/role assignment on the service connection's identity, or updating the target resource's access policy, followed by verifying the service connection and re-running.
questions.professionalAnswer: Nothing changed in the YAML is actually the clue that points me away from the pipeline entirely — if the pipeline logic were the problem, it would've been broken yesterday too. So I go straight to the service connection, and the first real move is just reading the actual error text carefully rather than assuming — Azure DevOps usually passes through the real Azure or AWS error, and that'll often tell you directly whether this is 'does not have permission to do X' versus something that smells like an expired credential. From there I check the service connection's own health in Project Settings, there's a Verify button that'll often catch this immediately rather than me guessing. The usual suspects, in order of how often I've actually seen them: somebody did an access cleanup and accidentally removed or narrowed the role assignment on the service principal backing this connection; the service principal's client secret hit its expiry date, which is sneaky because those are often set once at creation and nobody's watching a calendar for it; or the target resource itself — a Key Vault access policy, a storage firewall rule — got tightened by someone else entirely unrelated to this pipeline. The fix is basically never 'change the pipeline' — it's restoring the right role assignment, rotating an expired secret, or getting the target resource's policy corrected, then verifying the connection before just blindly rerunning the release and hoping.
questions.example: The error reads 'AuthorizationFailed... does not have authorization to perform action Microsoft.Web/sites/write' — tracing it back shows the service principal's Contributor role on the target resource group was removed two days ago during an unrelated access review, with no connection to anything in the pipeline's own YAML.
commonMistakes: Assuming the problem must be in the pipeline YAML since that's what the engineer owns, rather than investigating the external identity/access layer
Not reading the actual authorization error message closely before guessing at a cause
Not checking the service connection's own health/verify status directly
Fixing the symptom with a workaround in pipeline code instead of correcting the underlying role assignment, secret, or access policy
keyPoints: An unchanged pipeline failing at the authorization boundary points to an external identity/access change, not pipeline logic
The actual error message from the underlying cloud provider usually names the specific missing permission or expired credential
Common causes: removed/narrowed role assignment, expired service principal secret, or a changed target-resource access policy
The fix belongs in the identity/access layer, not in pipeline YAML

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons that an unchanged pipeline points to an external cause, not pipeline logic
Describes reading the actual error and checking service connection health as first steps
Identifies plausible real root causes (role removal, expired secret, access policy change)
Correctly locates the fix in the identity/access layer rather than pipeline code

questions.title: Canary Deployment Causing an Error Spike for a Slice of Users
questions.prompt: You've shipped a new version to 5% of production traffic as a canary. Error rates for that 5% have jumped noticeably, while the 95% on the old version remain normal. Walk through how you decide between rolling back and fixing forward, and what you do in the next few minutes.
questions.modelAnswer: The canary mechanism is working exactly as intended here — it caught a real regression while limiting exposure to 5% of traffic rather than 100%, and the decision in front of you is purely about next steps now that the signal has confirmed a problem. The default, correct first action in almost all cases is to roll back the canary immediately (shift traffic back to 0% on the new version, or scale it to zero / revert the routing), because the canary has already done its job of proving the new version is unsafe, and there is no benefit to leaving even 5% of users exposed to known elevated errors while a fix is investigated — 'fix forward' under live production error pressure is rushed, higher-risk work, and the old version is known-good and already warmed up and available. Fix-forward in place of rollback is only reasonable in narrow cases: if rolling back itself is unusually risky or slow for this specific service (e.g., a schema migration already applied that the old version can't handle), or if the fix is already identified, trivial, and faster to apply than a rollback would be — and both of those should be verified facts, not assumptions made under pressure. After rolling back, the investigation into the actual bug happens without the time pressure of live user impact, using logs/traces from the 5% affected canary pods, and a new canary is only attempted again after the root cause is understood and fixed, not patched blindly and re-shipped to see if it's better.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, the canary did exactly what it's supposed to do — it caught something bad before it hit everyone. The question in front of me isn't really 'is something wrong,' it's already answered; it's 'what do I do in the next five minutes,' and my default answer, almost every time, is roll it back. Not because fixing forward is never right, but because at the moment I've confirmed a real error spike, I don't have a diagnosed root cause yet, and shipping a fix I just wrote under live-incident pressure is a worse bet than reverting to the version I already know is fine and was running happily five minutes ago. The only times I'd seriously consider fixing forward instead are when rollback itself is the riskier move for this specific service — like if there's already been a database migration applied that the old version genuinely can't handle anymore — or the fix is already known, tiny, and clearly faster than a rollback would be. Those are facts I'd want to actually confirm, not something I talk myself into because I'm eager to not look like I broke something. Once I've rolled back, that's when the real investigation happens — pulling logs and traces specifically from those canary pods while they still exist, figuring out what actually broke, and the next canary attempt only goes out once I understand why the first one failed, not as a 'let's try again and see.'
questions.example: 5% canary traffic shows a 12% error rate versus 0.3% baseline on the stable version; rollback (traffic shifted to 0% on canary) within minutes, followed by root-cause analysis using the canary pods' logs before attempting a second canary with the actual fix.
commonMistakes: Treating fix-forward as the default response rather than rollback, under live user impact
Attempting a rushed fix without first confirming rollback is genuinely riskier for this specific case
Not preserving logs/traces from the affected canary pods before they're torn down during rollback
Re-shipping a new canary without having actually identified the root cause of the first failure
keyPoints: The canary mechanism succeeded by catching the regression at 5% exposure rather than 100%
Rollback is the correct default response under live user impact with an undiagnosed root cause
Fix-forward is only justified when rollback is genuinely riskier or the fix is already known and trivial
Root-cause investigation happens after rollback, using preserved logs/traces from the affected canary pods

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the canary as having succeeded at its job, not as a failure of the process
Defaults to rollback as the correct response to confirmed, undiagnosed live impact
Correctly identifies the narrow, fact-based conditions under which fix-forward would be justified
Describes sound follow-up root-cause investigation after rollback

questions.title: A Prometheus Alert Is Flapping and the On-Call Rotation Is Muting It
questions.prompt: An alert for 'elevated queue depth' has been firing and resolving repeatedly for days, and you discover the on-call engineers have started silencing it on sight without investigating, because it's 'always a false alarm.' How do you fix the underlying alerting problem, not just the immediate noise?
questions.modelAnswer: An alert that flaps repeatedly and gets silenced on sight is a sign that the alert's threshold, duration, or underlying signal doesn't actually distinguish 'needs human action' from 'normal, self-resolving variation' — and the dangerous part isn't the noise itself, it's that on-call has learned to distrust and auto-dismiss this specific alert, which risks them also dismissing it on the one occasion it's actually signaling a real problem. The fix starts with pulling the alert's actual firing history against the underlying metric's graph over the same period to see what the queue depth was actually doing each time it fired: if it's crossing the threshold briefly and self-resolving within normal processing time, the `for:` duration is probably too short relative to the system's normal recovery time, and should be lengthened so only a sustained breach fires. If the threshold itself is simply set too close to normal peak variation (e.g., queue depth routinely touches the threshold during expected batch jobs), the threshold needs to be reset based on what queue depth actually needs to reach before it represents a real, actionable backlog, ideally informed by what 'actionable' concretely means for this system (e.g., queue depth that will cause SLA-breaching processing delay if sustained). Beyond fixing this one alert, the broader issue — on-call silencing alerts on sight — needs its own conversation: it's evidence of alert fatigue that likely extends beyond just this one alert, and deserves a review of the team's overall alert set for other candidates with a similarly poor signal-to-noise ratio, not just a one-off fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: The alert being flaky is only half the problem — the part that actually worries me more is that on-call has started silencing it on sight, which means the alert has lost their trust, and the day it's genuinely trying to tell them something real, they're going to dismiss that too out of habit. So first I'd pull the actual firing history next to the real queue-depth graph for those same windows and just look — is it genuinely crossing the line and coming right back down within normal processing time, or is the threshold itself just sitting too close to normal peak noise, like whatever happens during an expected nightly batch job. Those are different fixes. If it's a brief, self-resolving blip, the `for:` duration is probably too short — stretch it so only a genuinely sustained backlog fires. If it's the threshold itself being too tight against normal variation, I need to actually figure out what queue depth means something real — like, what depth, sustained how long, would actually start causing an SLA breach — and set the threshold against that, not against a round number someone picked when the alert was first written. But I wouldn't stop at fixing this one alert. On-call muting things on sight is a symptom of a bigger alert-fatigue problem, and I'd use this as the excuse to go look at the rest of the alert set for other repeat offenders with the same bad signal-to-noise ratio, because this one probably isn't the only one teaching people to tune out.
questions.example: Queue depth graph shows repeated brief spikes to just above threshold during a nightly batch job, each resolving within 3 minutes as the batch completes; extending the alert's `for:` duration to 10 minutes stops it firing on the expected, self-resolving pattern while still catching a genuinely sustained backlog.
commonMistakes: Treating the fix as simply silencing or deleting the alert instead of correcting its threshold/duration
Not investigating whether the on-call team's habit of muting it has already generalized to other alerts (broader alert fatigue)
Setting a new threshold without first defining what queue depth level is actually operationally meaningful
Assuming a longer for: duration alone is always the right fix without checking whether it's actually a threshold problem instead
keyPoints: A flapping alert that on-call mutes on sight risks missing the one time it's actually real
Diagnosis requires comparing firing history against the actual metric graph to distinguish duration vs. threshold problems
The corrected threshold/duration should be grounded in what's actually operationally meaningful, not an arbitrary round number
The broader on-call muting habit should prompt a review of the full alert set, not just this one alert

Correctly distinguishes a duration problem from a threshold problem using actual data
Proposes grounding the new threshold/duration in genuine operational meaning
Extends the fix to a broader review of alert fatigue across the team's alert set

questions.title: Application Insights Shows Elevated Latency With Normal CPU and Memory
questions.prompt: Application Insights shows p95 response time has tripled over the past week, but CPU and memory on the hosting infrastructure look completely normal, and no recent deployment correlates with the change. How do you find the actual cause?
questions.modelAnswer: Normal CPU/memory with elevated latency points away from compute saturation and toward either an external dependency (a downstream API, a database, a third-party service) slowing down, or contention/waiting that doesn't show up as CPU usage (e.g., threads blocked waiting on I/O, lock contention, connection pool exhaustion) — none of which necessarily consume CPU while they're the actual bottleneck. The right next step is Application Insights' end-to-end transaction view / dependency tracking, which breaks a request's total time down into time spent in the app itself versus time spent waiting on each dependency call (SQL queries, HTTP calls to other services, cache calls); this directly shows whether the added latency is concentrated in one specific dependency call rather than spread generally across the request. If dependency tracking shows a specific downstream call's duration has grown, that redirects investigation to that dependency specifically — which may be an external team's service degrading, a database query whose execution plan changed as data volume grew (slow query, not slow app), or a connection pool that's become a bottleneck under current load even without high CPU. Since no deployment correlates with the change, a gradual, non-deployment-triggered cause (data growth degrading a query plan, a downstream dependency's own gradual degradation, growing connection pool contention as traffic has organically grown) is more likely than a code regression, which should shift where time is spent investigating.
questions.professionalAnswer: Normal CPU and memory is actually a useful negative signal here — it rules out the easy, obvious answer of 'we're just out of compute,' and points toward something that eats time without eating CPU: waiting on a dependency, a lock, a connection pool, a slow query, anything in the 'blocked, not busy' category. The tool I'd reach for immediately is App Insights' end-to-end transaction view — it breaks down where a request's time actually goes, in-app versus each dependency call, which turns 'latency went up' into something concrete like 'this one SQL call specifically went from 40ms to 800ms.' And since nothing in deployment history lines up with when this started, I'd specifically lean away from 'something we shipped broke this' and toward something that degrades gradually — a query whose execution plan quietly got worse as the table grew past some threshold, a downstream service someone else owns slowly getting worse on its own schedule, or a connection pool that's been fine for months and is only now hitting real contention because organic traffic has crept up. The dependency breakdown is what turns this from a guessing exercise into pointing at one specific, measurable thing, and from there it's a much narrower investigation — go look at that query's execution plan, or go talk to whoever owns that downstream service.
questions.example: Dependency tracking in the end-to-end transaction view shows a specific SQL dependency call's average duration grew from 45ms to 620ms over the same week, with app-side processing time essentially unchanged — redirecting the investigation to that query's execution plan rather than application code.
commonMistakes: Assuming normal CPU/memory means the app is fine and looking only at code-level changes
Not using dependency/end-to-end tracing to localize where the added time is actually being spent
Treating the lack of a correlating deployment as evidence the regression isn't real, rather than evidence it's gradual
Jumping to a conclusion about which dependency is slow without actually measuring it via the tracing data
keyPoints: Normal CPU/memory with elevated latency points toward waiting/contention rather than compute saturation
Application Insights' dependency/end-to-end tracing localizes where added time is actually spent
No correlating deployment suggests a gradual cause (data growth, downstream degradation, growing contention) rather than a code regression
Investigation should narrow to the specific dependency call shown to have grown, not a general guess

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interprets normal CPU/memory as ruling out compute saturation
Correctly proposes dependency/end-to-end tracing to localize the added latency
Reasons correctly about why no correlating deployment points to a gradual cause
Describes a concrete next step once a specific slow dependency is identified

questions.title: A CloudWatch Alarm Never Fires Despite a Clearly Breached Metric
questions.prompt: You can see in the CloudWatch metrics graph that a Lambda function's error count clearly spiked well above the alarm's threshold, but the alarm never transitioned to ALARM state and no notification was sent. How do you figure out why?
questions.modelAnswer: A visually obvious breach with no alarm transition points to a mismatch between what's graphed and what the alarm is actually evaluating, or an evaluation-period/data-treatment setting that doesn't match the error pattern's actual shape. The first thing to check is whether the alarm is configured against the exact same metric, statistic, and dimensions as the graph being viewed — a very common cause is the alarm watching `Sum` over a period while the dashboard graph is showing something else, or the alarm scoped to specific dimensions (a specific function version, alias, or resource) that don't match the instance that actually errored, causing the alarm's own data stream to show zero even while the dashboard's differently-scoped graph shows the real spike. Second, check the alarm's `evaluationPeriods` and `datapointsToAlarm` configuration against the error pattern's duration: if the errors spiked briefly and the alarm requires, say, 3 consecutive breaching datapoints to transition, a spike shorter than that requirement never accumulates enough consecutive breaching periods to fire, even though it's visually obvious on a finer-grained graph. Third, check 'missing data' treatment — some Lambda error-count metrics only emit a data point when an invocation actually occurs; if the alarm's missing-data treatment is set to 'treat as not breaching' or similar and invocations were otherwise sparse, that can suppress evaluation in ways that aren't obvious from the graph. Resolving this requires actually opening the alarm's own configuration (not just comparing visually to a dashboard) and checking its exact metric/dimension/statistic/period settings against reality.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fact that it's visually obvious on the graph but the alarm never fired tells me the alarm almost certainly isn't looking at the same thing the graph is showing, even if they look like they should be the same metric at a glance. First thing I'd actually open is the alarm's own configuration, not the dashboard — and specifically check the dimensions. A really common version of this bug: the alarm's scoped to a specific function alias or version, and the spike actually happened on a different version or on $LATEST, so the alarm's own metric stream genuinely stayed flat even while 'the function's error count' in a broader dashboard view spiked. Second thing, evaluation periods — if this alarm needs, say, 3 consecutive breaching data points to transition to ALARM, and the real spike was a short burst that didn't sustain across that many periods, it just never accumulates enough consecutive breaches, even though anyone eyeballing a 1-minute-resolution graph would call that an obvious spike. And third, I'd check how it treats missing data — Lambda error-count metrics sometimes only emit when there's an invocation at all, and if the alarm's missing-data setting treats gaps as 'not breaching,' that can quietly suppress things in a way that's not visible just looking at a line chart. Bottom line, I wouldn't trust the visual comparison alone here — I'd go read the alarm's actual metric math and settings line by line against what really happened.
questions.example: The alarm is scoped to `FunctionName=my-fn, Resource=my-fn:prod` while the spike occurred on an unaliased `$LATEST` invocation during a deployment — the alarm's own metric stream shows zero errors the entire time, even though the function-wide dashboard graph clearly shows the spike.
commonMistakes: Assuming the alarm is watching the same metric/dimensions as whatever dashboard graph was used to spot the problem
Not checking evaluationPeriods/datapointsToAlarm against the actual duration/shape of the error spike
Overlooking missing-data treatment settings that can suppress evaluation during sparse invocation periods
Comparing visually to a dashboard instead of directly inspecting the alarm's own configured metric math
keyPoints: A visible breach with no alarm firing usually means the alarm isn't evaluating the exact same metric/dimensions as what's graphed
evaluationPeriods/datapointsToAlarm must be checked against the real duration/shape of the spike
Missing-data treatment can silently suppress alarm evaluation during sparse-data periods
Diagnosis requires inspecting the alarm's own configuration directly, not just comparing visually to a dashboard

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies metric/dimension mismatch as a likely root cause
Correctly checks evaluationPeriods/datapointsToAlarm against the spike's real shape
Considers missing-data treatment as a plausible contributing factor
Proposes directly inspecting alarm configuration rather than relying on visual comparison

questions.title: Logs From an Incident Can't Be Correlated Across Services
questions.prompt: During a postmortem for a production incident spanning three microservices, the team discovers they can see each service's logs individually but cannot reliably tell which log lines across the three services belong to the same user request. What's missing, and how do you fix it going forward?
questions.modelAnswer: The missing piece is a shared correlation identifier (a trace ID or request ID) propagated across every service boundary for a given request, combined with structured logging that reliably includes that identifier as a queryable field on every log line, not buried in free-text messages. Without this, each service's logs are an isolated island — reconstructing a cross-service request path during an incident requires manually matching log lines by approximate timestamp and guessing at correlation, which is slow and unreliable, especially under concurrent load where many similar requests are interleaved in the same time window. The fix going forward has two parts: first, adopt a distributed tracing standard (OpenTelemetry is the standard choice) so a trace ID is generated at the entry point of a request and propagated through HTTP headers (or equivalent) to every downstream service call, with each service's instrumentation automatically attaching that trace ID to its spans; second, ensure structured logging (JSON or similarly structured log lines, not free-text) includes that trace ID as an actual field in every log entry, not just in trace spans, so logs and traces can be correlated and a single trace ID can be used to query logs across all three services in a centralized logging system. This turns incident reconstruction into a single query by trace ID rather than a manual timestamp-matching exercise.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's missing is dead simple to name and genuinely painful to retrofit: nobody's propagating a shared ID across the three services for a given request, so each service's logs are its own disconnected story, and reconstructing 'what actually happened to this one user's request' means manually eyeballing timestamps across three separate log streams and hoping nothing else happened at the same second — which, under real load, something always did. Going forward, this is exactly what distributed tracing is for — OpenTelemetry generates a trace ID at the front door and propagates it through every downstream call, so every service's instrumentation automatically tags its own spans with that same ID. But tracing alone doesn't fully solve it unless the logging side also picks it up — I'd want every service's structured logs to include that trace ID as an actual indexed field on every log line, not just present in the trace spans, so during the next incident, someone can take one trace ID and query logs across all three services at once and get back exactly the lines that belong to that one request, in order, instead of three separate searches and a lot of guessing. The investment here is genuinely annoying to make — every service needs instrumentation added and logging conventions changed — but the alternative is redoing this exact frustrating manual correlation exercise every single incident forever.
questions.example: With OpenTelemetry trace propagation and trace-ID-tagged structured logs in place, a single query `trace_id:"4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736"` against the centralized logging system returns the exact ordered set of log lines across all three services for that one request.
commonMistakes: Treating the problem as a logging-tool limitation rather than a missing correlation ID propagated at the application level
Adding tracing without also ensuring structured logs carry the same trace ID as a queryable field
Relying on timestamp-matching as an acceptable ongoing correlation strategy instead of fixing the root gap
Not recognizing that this retrofit requires instrumentation changes in every service, not a single central fix
keyPoints: The missing piece is a shared trace/request ID propagated across all service boundaries for a given request
Distributed tracing (e.g., OpenTelemetry) is the standard mechanism for generating and propagating that ID
Structured logs must also include that ID as a queryable field, not just the trace spans themselves
The fix requires instrumentation changes across every involved service, not a single centralized change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the missing shared correlation/trace ID as the root gap
Correctly proposes distributed tracing (e.g., OpenTelemetry) as the propagation mechanism
Correctly connects structured logging to carrying the same trace ID as a queryable field
Acknowledges the retrofit requires changes across every involved service

questions.title: Rotated Key Vault Secret Isn't Picked Up by Running Pods
